rt8f86.text: GL.iNet has confirmed that hackers exploited a vulnerability in its cloud remote management services to install custom malware on customers' routers and KVM devices, with some affected users reporting backdoors and reverse shells giving remote access to infected devices. GL.iNet manufactures networking equipment, including home and travel routers, as well as KVM devices that allow users to access and control computers remotely. Its GoodCloud platform allows customers to remotely manage supported devices, including accessing and controlling computers and servers connected to its KVM products. In a security advisory published on November 20, GL.iNet confirmed that an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in its cloud remote management services to access devices and install malicious software. "The attack path has been blocked. We fixed the cloud vulnerability and blocked the access used in this incident," the company said. "Devices can no longer be newly infected through this attack path. These measures do not remove malware from devices that were already infected." GL.iNet has not disclosed how the attackers exploited its cloud platform, how many customers were impacted, or whether information was stolen from compromised devices. The company is also investigating whether computers connected to infected KVM devices were compromised. GL.iNet recommends that customers check their devices for signs of infection and install the latest security firmware, even if no malware is detected. The company's initial instructions told customers to look for a process running as crond -i /tmp/.log, which GL.iNet said was an indicator of compromise. While the cloud vulnerability has been fixed, GL.iNet says stable firmware updates containing additional security fixes for both routers and KVM devices are scheduled for release on November 22, 2026. For KVM devices, customers can follow the company's firmware upgrade guidance, which recommends version 1.10.3 or later for the RM10, RM1, RM1V2, RM1PE, and RM4PE, version 1.10.3 beta or later for the RM10RC, and version 1.8.7 or later for the RMQ1. Router owners should install the latest security firmware for their specific model as soon as it becomes available. However, GL.iNet forum members warn that the company's detection instructions may not identify all compromised devices, including those infected with other backdoors or running reverse shells. GL.iNet has linked to a community-developed detection and cleanup tool as part of the company's official support instructions for routers and KVM devices. The scanner performs additional checks for known malware files, suspicious processes, modified system utilities, and configuration files modified for persistence. It can also collect forensic evidence and optionally remove known malware components. The project's developers warn that the scanner cannot detect every infection and that compromised devices may require reinstalling firmware without retaining existing settings, as malicious files stored in configuration directories could survive an ordinary firmware upgrade. Customers who suspect their devices were compromised should preserve evidence before resetting them, avoid restoring potentially infected configurations, and rotate credentials and access keys that may have been exposed. GL.iNet also asked customers who run the scanner to upload the anonymous report when prompted so the developers can determine the number and types of devices impacted. For KVM users, the malware may have allowed access to the computers controlled by the KVM, so those devices should also be analyzed for potential compromise. Malware and reverse shells discovered Following the disclosure, GL.iNet customers and security researchers shared evidence of custom malware infections designed specifically for GL.iNET devices, as well as root-level reverse shells that connected compromised routers to the IP address 170.39.226[.]219. The reverse shells used the Linux nc utility to create outbound connections, allowing remote attackers to execute commands on infected devices. Researchers at RemoteToHome Consulting also identified a potential command injection vulnerability in GL.iNet's GoodCloud client involving a handler used for AstroWarp/SD-WAN functionality. According to the researchers, the handler passes cloud-supplied values into shell commands executed with root privileges without properly validating them. However, GL.iNet has not confirmed that this particular vulnerability was used in the attacks. RemoteToHome says it analyzed 183 routers it owns or manages and found suspicious activity on 152, including 24 with root-level reverse shells, 47 with an older persistent backdoor, and 81 showing evidence that attacker-supplied commands had executed. The researchers note that their findings may not be the same as the other GL.iNet customers and that the older backdoor infections may not be linked to the November attacks. In a separate forum report, the owner of a compromised GL-RM1 KVM shared network logs showing it downloading a malicious ni.sh script and additional executable payloads from 66.245.219[.]252 on November 19. The owner also reported that the device began communicating with approximately 1,800 residential IP addresses daily and repeatedly contacted the TRON blockchain API, exhibiting activity suggestive of a peer-to-peer network. However, the purpose of these connections is unclear, and there is no confirmation that the compromised devices were being used as residential proxies or were part of a larger botnet. BleepingComputer examined a copy of the malicious ni.sh script [VirusTotal] and found that it contains code specifically tailored to GL.iNet routers and KVM devices. The script recognizes numerous GL.iNet device models and downloads malicious executables named gl-helper and gb from hardcoded servers. It also establishes persistence through startup scripts and scheduled tasks, allowing the malware to restart after a reboot or if its processes are terminated. The installer includes functionality to disguise the malicious process as crond -i /tmp/.log, matching the IOC published by GL.iNet. An interesting feature is replacing the legitimate netstat utility with a modified shell script that filters out connections to 66.245.219[.]252, potentially hiding the malware's communications from administrators examining network connections. The installer also contains functionality to install SSH public keys for remote access, modify file timestamps, and periodically contact a remote server to retrieve and execute commands. The attacker's infrastructure includes two IP addresses, 66.245.219[.]252 and 65.20.71[.]131, which match the IP addresses seen in the compromised KVM owner's logs. The script also contains Chinese-language developer comments describing its persistence mechanisms, reporting functionality, and interactions with GL.iNet's cloud management software, indicating a Chinese-speaking individual may have written it. Chinese-language comments in the ni.sh malware script Source: BleepingComputer BleepingComputer also examined a separate malicious Lua payload recovered from a GL-MT2500 router. The payload was launched through a modified urandom_seed startup script and included functionality to collect device information, contact remote servers, and download and execute additional programs. Malicious commands added to legitimate urandom_seed file Source: BleepingComputer Some of the malicious files recovered from GL.iNet devices had timestamps dating to December 2025, suggesting that some devices may have been compromised for months. However, it is unclear whether these infections involved the same threat actors or were related to the November 20 attacks. GL.iNet says it continues to investigate the incident and plans to notify identified affected customers using the email addresses associated with their cloud accounts. 7nygyq.text: E-commerce platform Cleverbridge is warning that hackers breached its systems and stole customers' payment card information, including credit card numbers and CVV security codes. Cleverbridge provides e-commerce services to software and SaaS companies, allowing them to sell products, process payments, and manage subscriptions. The company lists numerous technology brands as its customers, including Red Hat, SUSE, Tenable, Veeam, Jamf, Sony, and Parallels. However, it has not disclosed which businesses' customers were impacted by the breach. In a new page about the security incident, Cleverbridge says it detected unauthorized activity on November 4, 2026, and temporarily took systems offline to contain the breach. "All systems were brought back online on 4 November 2026; however, our investigation subsequently determined that a third party copied payment card data stored on our platform," reads the security incident disclosure. Cleverbridge began notifying affected customers on November 20, warning that hackers had stolen payment card details used to make purchases through its platform. While its public disclosure confirms the theft of payment card data, it does not specify which card details were stolen, instead referring affected customers to their individual notifications for more information. However, a breach notification shared with BleepingComputer reveals that the stolen information includes payment card numbers, expiration dates, and CVV/CVC security codes. "Based on our investigation to date, the information involved includes the payment card details you used to make a purchase through Cleverbridge, notably your card number, expiry date, card security code (CVV/CVC)," reads the notification. "Note however that no other personal data (for example your name, contact or billing details) were copied. The affected card ends in XXXX." BleepingComputer redacted the last four digits of the affected payment card. The company has not disclosed how the attackers gained access to its platform, how long they remained in its systems, or how many customers were affected by the breach. Of particular concern is the theft of CVV/CVC security codes, which are used to verify payment card transactions. Cleverbridge also confirmed that the incident was not a ransomware attack and that attackers did not encrypt any of its systems. The company says it has notified data protection authorities, law enforcement, payment card networks, and payment partners about the incident. Cleverbridge is also working with TransUnion's Cyberscout to distribute breach notifications and provide affected customers with complimentary credit monitoring and fraud assistance. Affected customers are told to review their payment card statements for unauthorized transactions. Cleverbridge also recommends contacting card issuers about the incident, as banks may decide to replace compromised cards. BleepingComputer contacted Cleverbridge with questions about how many customers were affected, how the attackers accessed its systems, whether the stolen payment card data was encrypted, and why CVV/CVC security codes were accessible. The company has not responded to our questions. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. y44w7c.text: Signal has announced new protections that block screenshots on iOS 27 and prevent AI assistants from capturing conversations on supported Android devices. The protections are designed to stop Siri and Gemini, the AI assistants built into iOS and Android, from accessing private conversations while performing tasks for users. The change comes after Signal introduced a feature in May 2025 that blocks Microsoft's controversial Recall screenshot-capturing feature on Windows 11. "We will now be taking similar measures to restrict agentic systems built into iOS 27 and on Android versions where we can detect an AI assistant attempting to read your Signal screen," Signal's president, Meredith Whittaker, said in a blog post. Whittaker says OS-level features such as Siri's Onscreen Awareness and Google's Gemini Intelligence can capture chat content as it appears on the app's screen, putting potentially sensitive private data outside Signal's control and exposing all conversation participants. Option to block Siri scanning on Signal for iOS Source: Signal Signal says its engineers spent months figuring out how AI systems access app data, designing targeted protections to block all extraction pathways verified through reverse engineering. However, Signal warns that AI agents could still access conversations through other methods, which Whittaker describes as "an existential threat to Signal." She explains that AI agents could access conversation data in multiple ways, as they are now embedded deep in operating systems, leaving apps vulnerable and with limited options for protecting users. The most notable example is macOS, where Signal says it's currently unable to provide any screenshot-blocking protection. For macOS 27 users, Signal recommends adding the app to the Excluded Apps list under System Settings > Siri to prevent Siri AI from proactively accessing message content. For this reason, Signal calls on Apple, Google, and Microsoft to fully disclose, through detailed documentation, all potential access mechanisms and give app developers a clear way to opt out of AI access across screens, files, notifications, and APIs. Signal did not provide specific app version numbers for the new protections but says they are automatically activated when possible. Signal recommends that users upgrade to the latest available version and go to Settings > App Security to check that Block Siri AI is enabled on iOS. On Android, Signal says it automatically enables Screen Security when it detects an AI assistant attempting to access the screen. However, on iOS, the protection also prevents users from taking screenshots of their Signal conversations, even for legitimate purposes. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. q63v93.text: Attackers stole data from inside three AI inference providers for months, and none of the three knew until researchers told them, the industrial cybersecurity company Dragos said this week. Some of the stolen requests were flagged as Zero Data Retention, the setting that is supposed to mean a prompt is never stored. OpenRouter, a gateway that routes customers' AI requests to a pool of third-party providers, said today that it has removed three providers from its platform, removed 125 endpoints from eligibility for Zero Data Retention, and notified all potentially affected customers. The findings showed no breach of OpenRouter itself, the company said. The earliest of the three breaches began in mid-July. The planted prompts were bait, but they were processed alongside real customer requests, and those were almost certainly copied too, the firm said. The finding comes from canary token research that seeded about two million prompts with unique web links and credentials between July and November, then watched for anyone using them. A planted secret can only be learned in one place, so any use of it means someone read the prompt that carried it. The largest of the three breaches involved a couple hundred AWS keys that were planted, each sent in exactly one request to one provider during a few short windows in late October. Every request sent during those windows was stolen, and some came from requests the provider had rejected before a model ever ran, indicating the attacker was copying traffic at the first point of arrival rather than deeper in the inference stack. The thief tested keys within hours in some cases, listed S3 buckets, searched Secrets Manager and Parameter Store, and tried to create Bedrock API keys and add IAM users to keep access, driving tens of thousands of AWS API calls. One attacker appears to have compromised two of the providers at once, using secrets from both from a single rented server. On November 1, the same attacker brought in ARTEX, an AI-driven penetration testing framework, and used it only to confirm that keys it already held were still live. Two of its user agents, artex-agent and artex-judge-r121, appear in no public indicator list the firm could find and are worth adding to detections. "A privacy flag doesn't help when the attacker is already inside," wrote HD Moore, the firm's chief research officer. The second finding needed no break-in. Sellers on an AI inference marketplace listed models at the lowest prices, enabled request logging, and collected what flowed through, the research found. The people doing it looked like individuals on home internet connections. One, working from a Mac on home broadband in France, took passwords from two prompts and typed root SSH login attempts by hand, then used the same machine to test several planted AWS keys. One of those keys had traveled through a different router that quietly forwarded some of its traffic to the marketplace, a hop that no customer was told about. That router has since told the firm it stopped, and route tracing across about 2,000 paths found several hundred unidentified systems, plus one seller that quietly adds about 1,000 hidden tokens to every prompt. A Chinese AI lab, which the research does not name, fetched the secret links from more than half of the seeded prompts sent to its models between July and October, including about two-thirds of the requests marked no data collection or Zero Data Retention. Prompts sent to U.S. hosting providers that resell the lab's models triggered the same scraper, thereby flowing back to the lab. A git client on another cloud later tried to clone private repositories referenced in the prompts, but only for that lab's models, and one large U.S. provider kept crawling a secret link more than two months after a single request to its search endpoint. Twenty-four days after one prompt was sent, its secret link was posted into a chat on Feishu, the Chinese workplace app known as Lark elsewhere. The link was opened within two minutes from three desktops and three phones in Beijing and Shanghai. The firm had disclosed only the first 8 characters of the provider's link, so whoever posted it was reading a cached copy of the full prompt. In practice, Moore wrote, the flagged prompts were kept, passed to other companies, and read by human beings. OpenRouter said in an incident announcement that the 125 endpoints removed from Zero Data Retention eligibility cover providers flagged by the researchers plus others cut as a precaution. Any endpoint removed during the review will require assurances and validation before its status is returned. The gateway is adapting the researchers' testing approach so that the checks can run on an ongoing basis and is verifying network paths to identify where requests and responses may be forwarded to third parties. The researchers are now working with about a dozen providers, and planted keys and secret links were still being accessed months after the first thefts, as of this week. Railway, a platform company, said in October that an intrusion it suffered was likely part of a series of attacks built to target platform companies with the end goal of compromising AI inference providers. Not all affected providers have posted publicly, the gateway said, and it has notified affected users either way. Three have posted. What the Providers Have Disclosed An attacker took control of an inference server at Phala and could view request data while it was being processed, the provider said in a preliminary incident report last week. The incident was contained on November 8, and the model service has been restored with added protections. Requests to the DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 model that reached Phala through the gateway between October 21 at 00:00 UTC and November 8 at 05:35 UTC should be treated as exposed, the report says, and every key, token, password, or other secret within them should be rotated. A third-party researcher had been placing unique canary credentials in requests since July 1, and only the ones sent on October 21 and 22 were later misused. Those tests sampled traffic rather than monitoring every request, so the provider maintains the broader precautionary window. At Together AI, an unauthorized party downloaded stored samples of customer prompts after an AI coding agent committed a credential to the company's public GitHub repository, the company said yesterday in a security notice. The samples had been collected for routine software testing and were generated by requests to the MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2, and Kimi K2.6 models in June and July. The party searched the samples for credentials to other services and tested them, and five of the tested credentials were canaries from the researchers' experiment. The company said it has no reason to believe the data went further, understands it has been deleted, and has made zero data retention the default for new accounts. Novita, another provider on the gateway, confirmed this week in a privacy notice that a routing configuration issue caused some MiniMax requests to be sent on to MiniMax's official API, beyond what was intended for those customers. Dragos has not named the three breached providers, OpenRouter has not named the three it removed, and neither has said publicly whether they are the same three. The provider behind the mid-July breach first blamed an internal misconfiguration, then a partner's data processing, before its own investigation found that attackers had compromised its internal credentials, the researchers said. It had still not disclosed the incident publicly as of this week. What Users Should Do The researchers' advice starts from one limit: a privacy flag binds only the first hop, Moore wrote, and AI agents will send whatever they can read, credentials included. Where a prompt goes is a choice, he wrote, and a customer who does not choose hands the choice to the lowest price. Self-hosting is the only option in which no third party reads a prompt, and going directly to a first-tier provider leaves one company, one contract, and one privacy policy to check. Routers need more care: pick the upstream providers yourself instead of accepting the default pool, verify that privacy settings actually change where requests go, and stay away from reseller marketplaces, some of whose capacity runs on stolen keys. A fake credential seeded into the context that agents and pipelines already send serves as a tripwire if any use of it is treated as an incident, and a free Thinkst Canarytoken is enough to get started. Settings that scrub known credential formats from prompts help too, though they miss sensitive data that is not shaped like a key.

1dwe0eu.text: A now-patched flaw in Ghostscript allows a crafted file to escape the program's security sandbox and run commands on the server that processes it. Ghostscript is the interpreter that many Linux servers use to convert uploaded PDFs, PostScript files, and images into other formats, often without the application calling it directly. Security firm pwn.ai showed this week that ordinary upload, preview, and print features in about ten common applications could be tricked into feeding it such a file. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-125396, was fixed on September 8, and there have been no reports of it being used in attacks. Getting a crafted file to Ghostscript is easy, because an application does not have to call it directly. A common image or document library such as ImageMagick, Pillow, libvips, or a Qt plugin will hand PostScript or EPS content to Ghostscript to render, even when the file is named .png, .jpg, or .pdf. A routine feature like making a thumbnail or cropping a picture can start the interpreter, and the exact path depends on the libraries the application uses. The underlying bug is a use-after-free in the part of Ghostscript that loads fonts. A crafted document uses it to switch off the checks in -dSAFER, the sandbox that is supposed to stop the document from running commands or reaching files. The security firm demonstrated the result by feeding such a document through about ten applications and watching a command run on the server, each time as the low-privilege account that does the rendering. Several of those paths needed no login: an anonymous print job to a shared Debian 13 queue, an emailed attachment that Roundcube webmail processed the moment the recipient opened the message, and public upload forms in the WordPress plugins Forminator and Essential Addons for Elementor. WordPress Core itself needed more: an account with the ability to upload files, which Authors and higher roles have by default. Although the CVE is classified as a local flaw, the firm's tests reached Ghostscript from the network via print jobs, email, and web uploads. The tested version and the access needed for each application are set out in its impact index. Artifex, which develops Ghostscript, fixed the flaw in version 10.08.0 on September 8, and is moving the vulnerable internal step into safer code. Ken Sharp, the developer who handled the fix, called that step "an ancient piece of code well known to be a vulnerability, but difficult to eradicate" in the bug report. The CVE was published last week and is scored 8.5 out of 10 in its security advisory. WordPress had already closed its own upload path in version 7.0.4 on August 12, under a separate identifier, CVE-2026-65640, as noted in its release notes. That fix and the Ghostscript fix cover different points in the same chain, so updating one does not remove the need for the other. Updating the Renderer The fix helps only where it reaches the renderer the application actually uses. Updating the host operating system does not update a separate copy of Ghostscript bundled inside a container image or an application, so a document worker can keep running the old code after the host package is replaced. Coverage across Linux distributions is uneven. As of last week, several still shipped a vulnerable Ghostscript or had a fix pending, according to the firm's survey. The list records package status, not a tested attack path for each system: Debian 12 (Bookworm): listed as vulnerable Amazon Linux 2, 2023, and 2027 Preview: fix pending SUSE Linux Enterprise 12 SP5 and parts of 15: fix in progress SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16.0 and 16.1: fix in progress openSUSE Leap 16.0 and 16.1: affected The firm did not establish whether current Red Hat, Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux, Oracle Linux, or stable Fedora packages carry the fix. Until the renderer is updated, the exposure can be reduced by requiring authentication on print queues and by limiting which file types an image processor accepts. System controls help too, and in one test an AppArmor profile stopped the compromised interpreter from starting a shell. One published proof-of-concept file, described in its technical analysis, shows only the core memory trick. It changes a value inside the running interpreter and sets it back, without running a shell command or touching files on the host, and on the patched 10.08.0 build it fails before that point. The firm's broader research extended to production services, including Google, which fixed the affected path last week. Its reports of similar problems at Dropbox and other unnamed services are separate Ghostscript bugs, not this one.

guedox.text: Rackspace warned customers that hackers breached its Rackspace Spot cloud platform using compromised credentials, allowing them to deploy unauthorized workloads and access Kubernetes secrets in customer clusters. Rackspace Spot is a cloud platform that allows organizations to deploy and manage containerized applications using Kubernetes. The company disclosed the breach in a notification sent to affected customers and obtained by BleepingComputer, stating that attackers accessed parts of the platform on November 17, 2026, between approximately 00:20 and 22:00 UTC. Rackspace says it learned of the intrusion on November 18 after receiving a customer report and confirmed that the recipient's organization was affected that same day. "On 17 November 2026 (about 00:20–22:00 UTC), an unauthorized party used leaked credentials to access parts of Rackspace Spot," reads the notification. According to Rackspace, the attackers were able to act as legitimate users in some customer organizations, allowing them to create pods in Kubernetes clusters, read Kubernetes Secrets, and list nodes and volumes. Kubernetes Secrets store sensitive information such as passwords, authentication tokens, and API keys that can be used to access databases, cloud services, and other systems. Rackspace warned that the attackers could have read any Secret stored in an affected user's clusters, as well as any Spot API tokens or refresh tokens held by that user. The company says it has since revoked affected tokens and sessions, removed the unauthorized pods, rotated keys, and strengthened access controls and monitoring. Affected customers have been instructed to reissue their Spot API tokens, replace refresh tokens used in automation tools, download fresh Kubernetes configuration files, and rotate credentials stored in their cluster Secrets. Rackspace also advised customers to analyze logs associated with databases, container registries, Git repositories, cloud storage, and third-party services dating back to November 17 to identify possible abuse of exposed credentials. The company shared the following indicators of compromise associated with the attack: IP address: 23.224.79.106 IP range: 23.224.0.0/15 Suspicious Kubernetes pod and object prefixes: i1, glm-, and probe BleepingComputer contacted Rackspace to ask how many customers were affected and whether customer data was stolen, but has not received a response. The breach also caused an extended outage of the Rackspace Spot administration console, temporarily preventing customers from managing their clusters and rotating potentially compromised credentials. In a Reddit discussion, Sirish Raghuram, co-founder and Chief Growth Officer of Platform9, which co-developed Rackspace Spot with Rackspace, explained that the company deliberately disabled access while securing its infrastructure. "I've been instrumental in creating Spot and in its operations to date, and I can tell you that the team and I are incredibly disappointed to have let you down in this way," Raghuram said. "I know you disagree, but we made the decision that shutting all access down and sanitizing the entire environment is what we can do to best protect everyone using Spot." After multiple delays, Rackspace announced that service had been fully restored on November 21. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. 161mlqr.text: Microsoft is warning organizations that it suffered a data breach after attackers exploited a vulnerability in its Entra Connect Health service to gain unauthorized access to administrator email addresses and tenant configuration information. Microsoft Entra Connect Health is a cloud-based monitoring service that allows administrators to monitor the health, performance, and alerts of their on-premises identity infrastructure through the Microsoft Entra admin center. According to a security notification sent to admins yesterday and shared on Reddit, Microsoft discovered the vulnerability in the Entra Connect Health API on November 9, 2026, after it was first introduced on July 23. An investigation determined that the flaw was exploited, allowing unauthorized parties to access tenant and service-monitoring metadata and potentially modify Connect Health monitoring configurations. "On 20 November 2026, we concluded our investigation and determined that unauthorized read-only access to tenant-level metadata associated with your organization had occurred. We did not identify any unauthorized configuration changes," Microsoft said in the notification. The company says the exposed information included: Email addresses belonging to tenant technical contacts and administrator accounts. Tenant IDs, display names, initial domain names, country codes, and regional information. Microsoft Entra license tiers and directory synchronization status, including whether synchronization was enabled and the last synchronization timestamp. Connect Health onboarding status. An expired certificate previously used to register Connect Health agents with a Microsoft internal service that was decommissioned in late 2024. Microsoft says the expired certificate was no longer in use but remained in Connect Health storage and was still returned by the API. However, the company says the vulnerability did not expose user passwords, password hashes, authentication tokens, valid cryptographic keys, on-premises server and Active Directory topology details, or Azure subscription information. Microsoft deployed a server-side fix on November 19 to prevent further exploitation and reviewed available telemetry to identify unauthorized API calls affecting customers. The company finished its investigation on November 20 and began notifying affected organizations. Microsoft has not disclosed how many organizations were impacted, but more than a dozen administrators have reported receiving the notification in the Reddit post. Some managed service providers (MSPs) also reported receiving notifications for multiple customer tenants, with one administrator saying the emails arrived hours apart. The notification says no software updates or other customer remediation are required to address the vulnerability. However, Microsoft recommends that organizations alert their security teams to potential targeted phishing and social-engineering attacks that could target the exposed administrator email addresses and tenant information. Organizations are also advised to ensure privileged accounts use phishing-resistant multifactor authentication, review their Connect Health configurations, and examine Microsoft Entra audit and sign-in logs for suspicious activity. Microsoft also published a PowerShell script at https://aka.ms/ConnectHealth/scripts that allows administrators to view the types of tenant metadata that could have been exposed. However, the script displays current configuration values rather than the information that was accessed during the breach. Microsoft has not disclosed who exploited the vulnerability, how many tenants were impacted, or when the attacks first began. When contacted by BleepingComputer, Microsoft confirmed that it had fixed the vulnerability and notified impacted customers. "We identified and addressed a security issue affecting Microsoft Entra Connect Health that could have resulted in unauthorized access to tenant-level contact and configuration metadata. We deployed a fix on November 19, 2026, and have notified impacted customers through Azure Service Health, providing guidance and support," a Microsoft spokesperson told BleepingComputer. Microsoft declined to provide further details about the breach. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. 1azlhxy.text: The BADBOX malware botnet has returned following last year's disruptions, generating a record 40 billion fraudulent advertising bid requests per day through infected Android-based devices. According to HUMAN's Satori researchers, who uncovered and disrupted the latest variant, BADBOX 3.0 had grown into the largest documented ad-fraud operation by daily bid request volume. BADBOX was first discovered in early 2023 on a T95 Android TV box bought on Amazon. In December 2024, Germany's cybersecurity agencies warned that the botnet had infected tens of thousands of devices. In March 2025, a large-scale disruption operation took place where HUMAN and Shadowserver cut off more than 500,000 BADBOX 2.0 devices from their control servers, while Google removed 24 apps that spread the malware from Google Play. Google later sued the botnet's operators, saying the BADBOX 2.0 had infected over 10 million Android-based devices by April 2025. BadBox returns However, the previous disruptions didn't stop the BADBOX operators from rebuilding the botnet and setting new records for daily fraudulent advertising bid requests. "At its height, BADBOX 3.0 accounted for roughly 40 billion bid requests a day and more than 4% of all CTV traffic observed by the Human Defense Platform," reports HUMAN. "BADBOX 3.0's volume was more than three times the volume of the previous record holder, VASTFLUX, and represents a larger peak than the last five years' worth of published Satori investigations combined." Bid requests volume Source: HUMAN The modus operandi remains the same: infecting cheap phones, tablets, and streaming TV boxes running the Android Open Source Project (AOSP) with malware that performs ad fraud and traffic proxying. The malware performs ad fraud by playing video ads in hidden windows while impersonating legitimate streaming apps to make the requests appear legitimate. HUMAN also observed fraudulent server-side ad insertion (SSAI) requests that tricked advertisers into believing ads were played on streaming devices, even though no actual device or video ad was involved. A proxying module also enrolled infected devices in one of 11 residential proxy networks without the owners' knowledge or consent. One of those networks, PXYEDGE, was identified as the rebranded successor to IpMoYu, a residential proxy service previously linked to BADBOX 2.0. The researchers say PXYEDGE advertised approximately 200,000 proxy nodes, while their monitoring showed unique connections peaking at around 340,000. HUMAN says some of the ad fraud traffic was also routed through these residential proxies to appear legitimate and evade anti-abuse filters. BADBOX operational overview Source: HUMAN The researchers linked the malware to a specific Chinese electronics manufacturer through its domains, device-specific checks in the code, a factory-installed TV launcher, and a repository maintainer. The infected devices fetch malware modules from public code repositories, while the same payloads are also mirrored across various hosting platforms for redundancy and to resist takedowns. HUMAN says it also participated in Google's disruption of the related XCPE malware operation earlier this month, which included taking down multiple C2 domains used by BADBOX 3.0. Additionally, one of the malware repositories was taken down, while HUMAN says its systems now filter fraudulent advertising traffic associated with BADBOX 3.0. However, HUMAN warns that the botnet operators are likely to adapt to the latest disruption, as they have done in the past. Users should only buy certified Android devices from reputable manufacturers and ensure that Play Protect is available and active. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. 1u90zlh.text: FBI systems have reportedly been breached for the second time in two months, this time targeting the agency's National Crime Information Center (NCIC), which is used to share information between local, state, and federal law enforcement agencies. The National Crime Information Center is an FBI-operated database used by law enforcement agencies across the United States to share information about wanted and missing persons, outstanding arrest warrants, stolen vehicles and firearms, protection orders, and other criminal justice records. Police officers routinely use the system during traffic stops, criminal investigations, and background checks. According to CNN's reporting, the FBI is investigating an apparent breach of the NCIC system, citing two people briefed on the investigation. The intrusion was reportedly discovered in recent days, although it is unclear when the breach occurred, how the attackers gained access, or whether any information was stolen. The FBI has not publicly confirmed the incident and did not respond to CNN's request for comment. The reported breach comes just two months after the ShinyHunters extortion group claimed to have breached the FBI's systems by exploiting an unpatched Oracle PeopleSoft vulnerability. The earlier attack targeted a third-party platform associated with the FBI's recruitment website, FBIJobs.gov, with ShinyHunters claiming to have stolen sensitive information from the agency's systems. The FBI subsequently launched an investigation that led to the arrests of suspected ShinyHunters members, including a Canadian cybersecurity executive reportedly linked to the attacks. There is currently no indication that the latest NCIC incident is connected to ShinyHunters or the earlier breach. It remains unclear whether the attackers accessed sensitive law enforcement records stored in NCIC or whether the intrusion affected the system's availability to law enforcement agencies. BleepingComputer contacted the FBI on Friday evening with questions about the reported breach but has not received a response. This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. pivlb6.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 21, 2026Vulnerability / Artificial Intelligence A malicious webpage could extract a Meta Muse user's private conversations and stored memories from the assistant without triggering any approval prompt, researchers have shown. The same attack could be extended to reach the credentials Muse stores for the user's connected accounts. The work was a laboratory demonstration, not an attack on real users, and it stayed inside the individual user's cloud machine. NebuSec, the security firm that published it yesterday, says Muse's team has since fixed every weakness it describes. Muse is Meta's personal AI agent, launched on September 8, that works through the online accounts a user connects to it and can make purchases on their behalf. Each person's agent runs on its own cloud computer. There, a monitoring layer called Sentinel is meant to be the single gate for anything the agent sends out, and the passwords and tokens for connected accounts are supposed to stay beyond the agent's reach. Muse's team described the aim at launch: "So we designed the system to assume the agent may be under attack and limit the potential damage." In the demonstration, a malicious page the agent opened could pull a user's conversation history and stored memories to an external server and alter them, with no prompt shown to the user, according to the firm's research write-up. From there, the researchers chained a flaw in Muse's built-in browser, which the assistant uses for tasks such as creating PDFs, to a Linux kernel flaw, thereby taking full control of the user's cloud machine. They set out that chain in a technical breakdown. That full control reached the credential store, the saved files, and Sentinel itself, the parts Muse's security design keeps walled off from the agent. The compromise went no further than that one machine. The researchers did not break out to the shared server beneath it or into other users' machines. Muse was built to assume its own agent could be turned against the user and to box in any break-in. Each of those controls worked as designed, the firm said, yet the attack still ran the whole way through. The firm says it reported the findings to Muse's team and that the exploits were all fixed before publication. Meta has not publicly confirmed the fixes or commented on the work, and the write-up does not say whether any user data was accessed before the patches went in. The firm's Muse research broke into the cloud system behind the assistant, unlike an earlier Muse flaw found in September, which only let malware already on a user's Mac hijack the assistant on the device.

1dc8sa6.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 21, 2026Vulnerability / Software Security A malicious OpenPGP key with an unusually long user ID can trigger a critical memory bug in GPGME, the standard library that programs use to work with GnuPG. The GnuPG project warned yesterday that the flaw could be used to steal data from affected applications and has released fixed versions. The bug, tracked as CVE-2026-129975, affects all software that uses GPGME before version 2.3.0, whether the library is loaded as a shared library, a Windows DLL, or statically linked into the program. Examples the project gives include most mail clients, many XMPP clients, Samba, and its own Gpg4win, GnuPG Desktop, and GnuPG VS-Desktop packages. The project has not reported any attacks exploiting the flaw, and it notes that remote code execution cannot be ruled out. Its example of a path to the bug is signed data sent to an application. Which programs pass such material to the library without a manual key import is not something the advisory says. The flaw is a double free, meaning the same memory is released twice. It sits in two routines, read_status() and read_colon_line(), that read status lines and key listings coming back from GnuPG. When the input runs long, the routines move the data to a larger buffer but record the new address only if they finish without errors. An error in between leaves a pointer to memory that was already freed, and cleanup then frees it a second time, as the project's tracker entry details. The flaw was found by Johan Carlsson and reported to the project by GitLab last week. Disclosure was set for November 25, the advisory says, and moved up because the new Ruby2Shell bug forced the company to update earlier. What to Update The fixed library version is GPGME 2.3.1, released this week. A version 2.3.0 was never publicly available. What to install depends on where the library sits: Shared library or DLL: update to GPGME 2.3.1, available from the project's official downloads and detailed in its security advisory. Windows: Gpg4win 5.1.2 bundles the fixed library. Its release notes call the issue severe and say to update as soon as possible. Older versions that cannot move to 2.3.1: the advisory carries a patch, and the legacy branch has its own fixed release, 1.24.4, whose legacy release notes say the project cannot guarantee that the branch will see every security patch. Bundled and statically linked copies: these are affected too, and updates to the system's shared library do not reach them, so the applications that contain them need their own rebuilt releases. GPGMEPP and GPGMEQT: no update is needed. The advisory offers no interim workaround for software that cannot update yet.

aqj2tu.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 21, 2026Artificial Intelligence / Cyber Espionage Suspected China-linked hackers used autonomous AI agents to find a previously unknown flaw in MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging server, and gain root access to a university server, Amazon Threat Intelligence said this week. The flaw allows an attacker with no account to write files outside the server's storage folder, and it affects MONAI Label 0.8.5 and earlier in the default setup, which runs with no login enabled. The maintainers have merged a fix in the source code, but there is still no fixed version to install. MONAI Label is a server that research teams use to label medical scans and train imaging models; it is a separate program from the broader MONAI framework. The weakness is a path-traversal flaw in the parts of the server that store uploaded images and labels. A file identifier supplied by the caller is appended to the storage folder and written to disk without checking that the result remains within that folder. The server writes with the privileges of the account it runs under, so an attacker cannot write anywhere on the machine, but a writable code or settings location can open a path to running code. Authentication is off by default, so any client that can reach the server over the network can set off the write. Versions 0.8.5 and earlier are affected. Amazon reconstructed the intrusion after finding the operator's own Cairn control panel sitting on the internet without a password. Cairn is an open-source framework that runs AI agents as automated penetration testers, and the exposed panel revealed the agents' task settings, prompts, and run history. Over about 48 hours in September, the agents mapped the application's interface and reached the point of writing files to the server in roughly 11 minutes, the company said in its incident report. The agents worked with little step-by-step direction. The operator set the goal of getting shell access and chose the targets, and the agents selected the methods themselves, according to the company. Investigators tie the campaign to a China-linked actor with moderate confidence, pointing to Simplified Chinese prompts, China Standard Time settings, and targets likely of interest to China. They did not connect the work to a named group or establish that a government was behind it. A root shell came later, and not within those 11 minutes. In a separate session, the agents used the same flaw to plant a file that Python runs automatically at startup. They then triggered a training feature that started a new Python process, which loaded that file and connected back to the attacker as root. That root access was on one university server, and whether another MONAI Label system would give the same result depends on how it is run and what its service account can do. In a later session, the operator handed the agents a tunnel into a second university network running the same software. Amazon believes the network was broken into in the same way but has not confirmed the second compromise. The maintainers confirmed the flaw and merged the source fix on October 19, which forces uploads to resolve inside the approved folders and rejects empty names or names that begin with a dot. Their security advisory, published earlier this week, still lists no patched version and says the correction will arrive in a future release. The newest release listing remains 0.8.5, which dates to 2024. A merged fix in source code is not the same as a package you can install. The flaw is now listed in the CVE record as CVE-2026-133968, published this week and rated 9.8 out of 10, a critical score. The project's advisory still shows no CVE assigned, which is a lag in updating that page, not a sign of a second flaw. What to Do Now With no fixed release available, the practical steps are to cut off exposure and limit what a compromised server could reach: Block untrusted network access to MONAI Label servers with firewall and routing rules, not just hard-to-guess URLs. Turn on authentication, which the server leaves off by default. Run the server under a limited account rather than root, and restrict the folders it can write to. Do not assume a source build is safe. Confirm it includes the October fix before treating it as patched. If a server was reachable, check for unexpected Python startup files and unusual training jobs, the path the reported attack used. The company's account is based on its own reconstruction and has not been independently confirmed. It does not show that patient scans or records were taken, that clinical systems were touched, or that the attacker reached past the university targets described. The campaign also included failed operations, and the root result on one server should not be taken as the outcome for every MONAI Label deployment.

10d76gs.text: Signal has announced that it will restrict screenshots by default to stop artificial intelligence (AI) agents from reading private chats on Android and iOS devices, but conceded that the protection is "incomplete." The feature applies to agentic systems built into iOS 27 and on Android versions where the encrypted messaging platform can detect an AI assistant attempting to read the Signal screen. It also builds upon a similar setting that Signal introduced in Windows 11 last May following Microsoft's release of the controversial Recall feature. Calling the agentic integrations into Android, iOS, and Windows an "existential threat to Signal," Meredith Whittaker, president of the Signal Foundation, said the move is designed to uphold its privacy guarantees in the AI era. "In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents 'scan' the information that's on your screen," Whittaker said. "In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding." "The net result is that these AI capabilities in the operating system are undermining Signal's ability to independently guarantee privacy." The risk here is that AI agents can capture and store the information accessed from Signal either locally or on remote servers, with the activity occurring outside of the platform's control and potentially putting the privacy of all the participants in a conversation at risk. Users who want to disable the option can do so by navigating to Settings > Privacy > App Security > toggle "Block Siri AI" (on iOS) or "Screen security" (on Android). "However, doing so will potentially expose your (and your contacts') Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees," Signal said. "Our remedy is also incomplete – while we are doing everything we can, restricting screenshots does not address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data, such as retrieving content already present on a user's device via the file system." Signal also pointed out that application developers lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from eroding application-level privacy. It also called out the companies for failing to provide adequate documentation about how these systems work to help design necessary controls to prevent the agents from accessing sensitive application data. Specifically, it's urging the tech giants to provide "two common-sense remedies" to help protect the privacy of its users - Access to easy and well-documented way to opt their app out of AI data access and processing entirely, including screen reading, filesystem access, notifications, APIs, and other OS frameworks, without making drastic compromises to the core user experience Create better documentation and technical specifications around how AI agents function, specifically with regards to data access and processing The concerns are not theoretical. Reuters recently reported that Muse, Meta's AI agent, was able to bypass its own official "Connector" tool to obtain access to Signal messages on both an Apple computer and an Android device by taking advantage of the broad operating system permissions granted to it during initial setup. On macOS, for example, the agent leveraged macOS's accessibility and screenshot tools to navigate to the Signal app, take screenshots, extract text from those images, and regenerate the textual content within the Muse app. On Android, it read messages by abusing its access to the device's push notifications. In one case highlighted by the news agency, the AI agent alerted a Meta staffer using Muse on her personal phone with a reminder to respond to a message from her sister on Signal. "This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this," the employee said in an internal post. "We also see a growing need for tools that can prevent third-party agents, like Meta's Muse, from accessing application data using the deep permissions that users are encouraged to grant them during setup," Whittaker said. "In many cases these agents are leveraging accessibility settings that were meant to empower actual people to get the most out of their apps and services, not to act as a skeleton key that provides access to AI agents." Late last month, Apple released iOS 27.2 with an "Excluded Apps" option that lets users choose which apps Siri, Search, and suggestions can access. With Google Gemini, users have the ability to disconnect apps via the Connected Apps settings. Earlier this week, the iPhone maker also previewed new controls that allow Mac users to give more granular access to data they give to apps, including those that use artificial intelligence (AI) agents.

19fccy5.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 21, 2026Vulnerability / Enterprise Security The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Friday added four flaws impacting Apache Roller, Cisco Expressway, SAP NetWeaver, and Broadcom VMware vCenter to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV), citing evidence of active exploitation. The vulnerabilities are listed below - CVE-2026-129448 (CVSS score: 9.8) - A deserialization of untrusted data vulnerability in Apache Roller that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code via the XML-RPC endpoint, which accepts and deserializes vendor extension types before authentication. (Fixed in November 2026) CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS score: 9.8) - A use of hard-coded credentials vulnerability in Cisco Expressway Series that could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker with persistent cookies and network access to execute commands as root on a clustered device via the database service. (Fixed in October 2026) CVE-2025-42884 (CVSS score: 6.5) - An improper neutralization of special elements in data query logic vulnerability in SAP NetWeaver Enterprise Portal that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to disclose or modify server information via injected JNDI environment properties or a URL used during JNDI lookup operations. (Fixed in November 2025) CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An authentication bypass using an alternate path or channel vulnerability in VMware vCenter that could allow an unauthenticated attacker with network access to vCenter to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system. (Fixed in November 2026) Earlier this week, the maintainers of Apache Roller acknowledged that the "issue is being actively exploited" but did not reveal how it was being weaponized or who is behind it. As of writing, there also appear to be no public reports documenting active exploitation of CVE-2025-42884. The addition of CVE-2026-76466 to the KEV catalog follows a report from F6 that the vulnerability was exploited to breach a Russian organization following the release of a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit, enabling the attackers to move laterally across the network and access sensitive data. The activity has not been attributed to any threat actor. The exploitation of CVE-2026-123890, on the other hand, has linked to a suspected China-nexus cyber espionage group tracked as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221), which is said to have weaponized it in conjunction with another now-patched flaw in BeyondTrust Remote Support (CVE-2026-102764, CVSS score: 9.3) to deploy custom backdoors for persistent access and data theft. Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies have been urged to patch all four vulnerabilities by November 23, 2026, pursuant to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk.

1ghlyk1.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 20, 2026Vulnerability / Mobile Security Meta-owned WhatsApp has addressed security vulnerabilities, including one impacting its Android app that it suspects may have been exploited in connection with scam messages. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-23871, has been described as a case of incomplete validation of external ad-reply URLs in WhatsApp for Android and WhatsApp Business for Android before 2.26.17.4. The issue could have "caused a target's device to reveal its IP information to an attacker if an attacker sent media from an attacker-controlled URL when a crafted Click to WhatsApp ad-reply message was rendered and displayed in a message thread," WhatsApp said. The messaging platform said it may have been "abused in conjunction with specific spam messages." Internal researchers on the WhatsApp Security Team have been credited with discovering and reporting the issue. When reached for comment, a WhatsApp spokesperson told The Hacker News that the vulnerability was discovered while disrupting a scam campaign. "We believe a scammer was using it to make their scam message seem more credible," the spokesperson added. WhatsApp did not disclose the scale of the activity, and if those efforts were successful. Also addressed by the company are two other flaws - CVE-2026-102769 - An SQL injection vulnerability in WhatsApp for Android prior to version 2.26.35.74 that occurred when a recipient tapped on a specially crafted "order details" message sent from an unofficial client, causing locally-stored WhatsApp files to be deleted. CVE-2026-44908 - A trust-validation vulnerability in WhatsApp's certificate verification mechanism for Meta AI's confidential computing infrastructure that affects WhatsApp for iOS before 2.26.24.72, WhatsApp Business for iOS and WhatsApp for Mac Desktop before v2.26.23.72, WhatsApp for Android before v2.26.23.74, and WhatsApp Business for Android before v2.26.23.70. Interestingly, CVE-2026-102769 is also capable of leaking one bit of information through a timing-based side channel if the user is online at the time of receipt of the malicious message. It "leaked one bit of information asked by the attacker about the user's chat database via an induced-crash delivery receipt timing side channel," WhatsApp added. There is no evidence the vulnerability has been exploited in the wild. Successful exploitation of CVE-2026-44908, on the other hand, could have allowed a bad actor positioned within Meta infrastructure to bypass the hardware root of trust using a Versioned Chip Endorsement Key (VCEK) certificate not signed by the hardware manufacturer's key. "Any such VCEK Cert would first have to be published to the third-party binary transparency ledger used by WhatsApp Private Processing," WhatsApp noted. "The ledger shows that every published VCEK certificate chains to the hardware root of trust, confirming no exploitation." WhatsApp is advising users to keep their apps and devices up to date to ensure optimal protection. The company also said that it continuously works to strengthen its systems and acknowledged the bug bounty community's contributions towards keeping the platform secure.

fb56hx.text: Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a previously unknown Android malware framework called Bazuka that offers large language model (LLM) integration for victim management and control at scale. Dutch mobile security company ThreatFabric said it discovered the threat in late October 2026 during an investigation into an NFC-relay banking Trojan. "Bazuka is a full malware framework," ThreatFabric said in a technical report. "A dropper/downloader, a core, and 23 modules cover overlays, keylogging, 2FA and SMS interception, remote control, and crypto-address swapping." One notable aspect of the malware that distinguishes it from the rest is a novel overlay technique that allows the trojan to take a screenshot of the home screen or lock screen, and display that as an overlay on demand to cover up malicious activities taking place in the background. Another perhaps not-so-surprising element is the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in the control panel to help operators identify victims of interest and manage infections. It supports both locally hosted models and models accessed through an API. One of the sample prompts provided by the author refers to a score, indicating an operator can likely request the AI model to score victims and determine how attractive they are as targets. The panel also supports the following capabilities - Create accounts for traffers, who are cybercriminals responsible for driving victims to malware using various lures Build droppers containing the malware with options to choose the kind of permissions specified in the Android manifest file likely in an attempt to bypass Google Play app review process This indicates that the dropper apps can be distributed via at least two distribution channels: through traffers, who can use social media ads or bogus sites to trick users into downloading them, and Google Play Store. One of the droppers containing the malware masquerades as a premium, adult-friendly version of TikTok (package name: "com.tiktok.premium"). Two different variants of the Bazuka attack chain have been observed - A dropper, which asks the victim for permissions to install applications from third-party sources and then proceeds to download a standalone APK ("com.tiktok.premium.pro") that serves as the stager A downloader that directly downloads the main payload It's suspected that the stager is the same as the downloader, whose main responsibility is to retrieve the core and supplementary modules necessary for a particular campaign, and then launch them. "Once the core and required modules are loaded, Bazuka operates as a keylogger and a classic overlay trojan, monitoring the text entered by the victim and displaying an overlay at the right moment," ThreatFabric said. "All functionality is controlled by commands from C2 [command-and-control]." The core module is the orchestrator, maintaining communication with C2, loading additional DEX modules, dispatching commands, collecting device information, and managing permissions and component updates. Like other Android trojans, it abuses Android Debug Bridge (ADB) shell commands and the operating system's accessibility services to request permissions and grant them automatically. "Important components of the core include mechanisms for enabling Wireless Debugging and completing the pairing process," ThreatFabric explained. "The core can open the system settings screen, find the relevant menu, enable Developer options, and then enable Wireless Debugging." "When this mode is enabled, it also intercepts the PIN, which is then used to establish a TLS connection to the ADB daemon." Furthermore, the core component counters detection by Google Play by disabling the protection component through the accessibility services API. It is also equipped to launch a self-destruct mechanism that clears local storage, deletes the database, and disables the application completely. Communication with the C2 server takes place over two WebSocket channels - Control, which is used to issue commands Data, which is used to exfiltrate data and screen capture streams Bazuka supports 23 modules that enable comprehensive data and cryptocurrency theft - call_forwarding, to manage call forwarding through USSD commands clip_monitor, to act as a clipper and substitute cryptocurrency wallet addresses copied to the clipboard with attacker-controlled ones contacts, to collect contact information device_control, to manage the device over the ADB bridge and execute commands as shell commands file_manager, to access the file system input_recorder, to act as a keylogger and capture all text entered into a target application, as well as identify bank card numbers, wallet addresses, and passwords in user input location, to determine a victim's location using GPS, cell tower positioning, and Wi-Fi media, to capture photos and stream camera video and microphone audio oem_power, to open system and OEM settings for power saving, background operation, and autostart optics, to facilitate remote control, screencasting, and phishing overlays preflight, to perform preliminary checks of the runtime environment proxy, to implement a reverse TCP proxy push, to create and manage local Android notifications screen_control, to capture the lock screen PIN, text password, and unlock pattern through accessibility services self_adb, to implement an embedded ADB client session_ui, to display phishing HTML overlays smsmessage, to access SMS messages and extract potential verification codes, send SMS messages, and attempt to delete messages from the device system_checker, to check the runtime environment and implement anti-analysis measures tapread-nfc_module, to interact with contactless bank cards toast, to display text messages on the device's screen twofa, to capture one-time verification codes uninstall_shield, to counter attempts to uninstall or force-stop the application ussd, to send USSD requests from the victim's device and receive responses from the mobile operator The malware has not been attributed to any known threat actor or group. However, the panel has been found to display UI elements in a mix of English and Russian. "ADB bridging is becoming a standard feature of modern banking trojans," ThreatFabric said. "While it is not there yet for Bazuka and its current architecture, this is a very concerning sign, as it allows malware to obtain various privileges covertly and deploy independent modules that can survive removal of the host application." "Another equally concerning feature is the use of LLM chats directly within the control panel. AI agents are used to identify victims of interest." ArcticRAT Android Malware Uses LLMs to Extract High-Value Data Bazuka is not the only Android-focused threat to integrate LLM. Last week, Zimperium zLabs research team detailed another sophisticated and rapidly evolving Android malware called ArcticRAT that supports 129 distinct commands and incorporates LLM APIs into its data exfiltration pipeline to extract high-value financial intelligence from stolen SMS messages and app data. "What initially began as a targeted spyware operation aimed at users of 11 specific cryptocurrency apps has morphed into an enterprise grade, AI-powered, Remote Access Trojan (RAT)," researchers Rajat Goyal and Fernando Ortega said. Infection chains make use of malicious sites impersonating Google Play app listings to convince users to install the dropper app. Unsuspecting users are redirected to these pages through malvertising, smishing, or third-party forums. The apps masquerade as popular brands (e.g., Amazon and TikTok), cryptocurrency applications, and generic file managers. Once installed, the app abuses Android accessibility services to establish remote control, automate fraudulent activity, and leverage AI to parse and "clean" exfiltrated data. It uses TCP sockets to communicate with the C2 infrastructure. An initial reconnaissance step is used to build a host profile, which then dictates the C2 server to dynamically select the relevant attack payloads to deploy. At a high level, the malware supports the following features - Initiate a real-time video transmission from the compromised device Abuse accessibility services for full remote control Serve fake extortion overlays and deceive victims into making cryptocurrency payments Make use of LLMs to process harvested SMS messages and look for financial, banking, and trading apps through hard-coded prompts that ask the model to take the role of a professional SMS analyzer and device app analyzer, respectively Capture credentials, authentication codes, and private communications Serve overlays to steal device lock screen pattern, PIN, or password "The malware requests VPN service privileges to null-route network communication on the victim's device, effectively blinding Google Play Protect telemetry during the staging phase," Zimperium said. "To prevent the user from interfering with these operations, ArcticRAT employs a defense evasion tactic known as a "Black Screen" overlay. When the attacker is navigating banking apps via Hidden VNC (HVNC) or auto-approving system permissions, the malware draws a completely black, un-dismissible view over the screen and drops the brightness to zero. To the victim, the device appears locked or powered off." Recent versions of ArcticRAT have also been found to abuse the native Wireless Debugging mechanism to initiate a privileged shell session on the victim machine and execute commands, including enabling or disabling accessibility permissions, verifying lock screen PIN or pattern, and displaying a black screen to conceal background operations. "By abandoning hardcoded attacks in favor of real-time Hidden VNC (HVNC), raw TCP command-and-control (C2), and aggressive defense evasion overlays, the malware achieves complete device takeover," Zimperium said.

1rwvmxm.text: A flaw in KVM, the hypervisor built into the Linux kernel, let researchers read about 127 GB of a cloud server's memory from inside a virtual machine of their own on DigitalOcean. On a shared server, that memory can include other customers' virtual machines. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-99312, affects only hosts with AMD processors and nested virtualization enabled. Fixed kernels shipped upstream on Tuesday, the day before the research went public. The provider patched its own fleet with a live patch, telling Droplet customers: "No action needed on your part." Operators who run their own KVM hosts on AMD hardware need to update the host kernel or turn nested virtualization off. Oren Yomtov, a researcher at the security firm Terra Security, found the flaw and reported it through the provider's bug bounty program. The provider confirmed the exploit worked on its own hosts and treated it as critical, and the Linux KVM maintainers, told on October 21, merged a fix on November 2. In the test on one of its Droplets, the first thing to come back was the host's kernel version banner, followed by about 127 GB of the host's RAM, mapped read-only, the provider said in a disclosure post yesterday. The write test ran on the researchers' own bare-metal AMD server, with no other customers attached. There, the guest wrote 32 chosen bytes into a live page of the host kernel's memory, and a witness module loaded into that kernel confirmed the change. Both tests started with root access inside a VM controlled by the researchers. An attacker would need the same position: control of a guest on a vulnerable host, not just network access to it. Intel-based KVM hosts are not affected, because the vulnerable code exists only in KVM's support for nested virtualization on AMD. Many cloud providers the researchers surveyed were not vulnerable because they had not enabled nested virtualization on AMD. There are no reports of the flaw being used outside research, according to VirtFusion, a virtualization platform vendor that is tracking the issue for its operators. No exploit code has been published either, and no guidance exists for detecting a past attempt. Severity ratings disagree. The Linux kernel's CVE team scores the flaw 8.8 out of 10, with high impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability, while Red Hat's preliminary security assessment rates it as Moderate at 5.6 and treats the impact as denial-of-service only. The provider treated it as critical for its own shared cloud. Terra's technical analysis, published on Wednesday, describes a pointer left pointing at freed memory. KVM confines each VM with a table, the nested page table, that translates the VM's memory addresses into the host's real memory, and the processor finds that table through a pointer kept for each virtual CPU. Some hosts let a VM run a VM of its own, a nested VM. When a reset signal called INIT stops the nested VM, KVM skips restoring the outer VM's pointer, leaving it pointing to a page of memory the kernel has already freed. Once the kernel reused that freed page, the guest could fill it with entries of its own choosing, and the processor followed them as if they were the real table. The forged entries could name any physical page on the host, which is how about 127 GB of the server's RAM came into reach of a guest that was never given it. The fix makes KVM reset that memory-management state on every INIT. The flaw was created by a security fix. A 2022 patch for a different nested-virtualization bug, CVE-2022-3344, switched a reset path back to the outer VM's control block but missed the page-table pointer, the researchers say, and the error then sat in the kernel for just under four years. In earlier work called PatchSlop, the team found that the fix for another one introduced 3.2% of kernel vulnerabilities. What to Do The fix lives in the host kernel. Updating the operating systems inside the VMs changes nothing, and a host keeps running its old kernel until it is rebooted. Upstream, the fix shipped on Tuesday in stable kernel 7.3.5 and in the long-term kernels 6.18.64 and 6.12.118, the kernel team's CVE announcement shows. The affected code goes back years: it entered the 6.1 kernel in 2022 and was carried into the 5.15.81 and 6.0.11 releases, so older kernel lines and the distribution kernels built on them are in range. Distribution kernels mostly do not have the fix yet. As of publication, Debian's security tracker lists the kernels in all of its releases as vulnerable, with a fix only in unstable, and Ubuntu's CVE tracker rates the flaw High and lists its kernels as vulnerable with no fixed package released. Red Hat lists the Enterprise Linux 9 and 10 kernels as affected with the fix deferred, and the Enterprise Linux 8 kernel as not affected. Until a fixed host kernel is installed and the host rebooted, the only available protection is to turn nested virtualization off. That closes this path completely, but VMs can then no longer run VMs of their own, so warn tenants who depend on that before making the change. Nested virtualization is on by default in the kernel's kvm_amd module, according to VirtFusion's operator guide, so an unpatched host is exposed unless the setting was deliberately changed. To check and change it: Check the setting with cat /sys/module/kvm_amd/parameters/nested. A value of 1 or Y means nested virtualization is on. If the host cannot be updated yet, add options kvm_amd nested=0 to the host's module configuration. Reboot the host. The setting cannot change while VMs are running, and a newly installed kernel does not protect the host until the reboot either. Confirm with uname -r and by reading the nested setting again. The flaw is the latest in a series of KVM isolation failures disclosed this year, after a 16-year-old flaw in KVM's shadow memory management that affected both Intel and AMD systems, and the PwnEscape flaw in Linux's networking code, which let a guest read host memory in Vercel's live sandboxes in October.

91ebfq.text: Security leaders are about to hand AI agents a lot more authority. In a recent a16z survey of CISOs at organizations with more than 1,000 employees, 36% said they are comfortable today letting AI agents act autonomously on low-risk security actions. In 12 months from now, 60% expect to be comfortable at that level. Overall, AI SOC was the highest ranking initiative for 2027. The pressure behind the shift is easy to see. In the same survey, the most common worry was AI-accelerated attacks outpacing the team's ability to respond, selected by 55% of respondents. Analyst time is the scarcest resource in the SOC, and every alert still means pulling evidence from several systems, reconstructing what happened and deciding whether it matters. The same respondents are cautious at the top end. Only 1% are comfortable with agents acting autonomously on most actions today, and only 7% expect to be a year from now. Most teams want more autonomy, just not all of it. Discussions today frame autonomy as a single slider that runs from "AI suggests" to "AI acts," and that exact framing is why so many programs stall. Autonomy is a set of decisions made per stage of the workflow and per action, and the teams that get it right treat it as something an agent earns with evidence. Autonomy is not “all or nothing”, but rather a spectrum The question "how much do we trust the AI" is too broad to answer. Researchers worked this out decades ago, in a framework later applied widely in aviation and air traffic control, long before anyone was building SOC agents. In a widely cited 2000 paper, Parasuraman, Sheridan and Wickens proposed that automation applies to four broad functions. Those are information acquisition, information analysis, decision and action selection, and action implementation.
