q9080h.text: Austria's Foreign Ministry said late last week that hackers breached one of its websites and accessed the names and official contact information of employees at its Vienna headquarters and at Austria’s diplomatic missions abroad. The breach occurred between November 12 and 13 and affected a website operated by an external service provider, according to a ministry statement reported by public broadcaster ORF on Friday. The ministry said the breach had been contained and that no personal information belonging to members of the public was compromised. The hackers have not been identified, and it remains unclear how they gained access to the website or whether they stole any information. The ministry said it was taking the incident "very seriously" and had notified Austria's cybersecurity and data protection authorities. A spokesperson told Recorded Future News: “For security reasons, we do not disclose details of specific technical vulnerabilities or security measures. The incident has not been attributed to any particular actor.” The attack coincided with a global Microsoft service outage that disrupted several of the company's services for approximately 24 hours. Microsoft attributed the disruption to a software bug and infrastructure failures. Austrian authorities have not established whether the two incidents were connected. Austria's Foreign Ministry has previously been targeted by suspected state-sponsored hackers linked to Moscow. In late 2019 and early 2020, the ministry suffered a cyberattack that lasted several weeks and was described by Austria's National Security Council as a targeted intelligence-gathering operation. In July 2026, Vienna publicly attributed the attack to Russia. The latest breach comes amid worsening diplomatic relations between Austria and Russia. In October, Vienna expelled four Russian diplomats, bringing the number of Russian diplomatic personnel declared persona non grata by Austria since 2020 to 18. Tensions escalated further last week after a Russian drone strike damaged the Austrian Embassy in Kyiv. Austria condemned the strike as "unacceptable" and "a violation of international law," and Foreign Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger summoned Russia's ambassador in Vienna. There is no public evidence linking Russia to the latest cyberattack. Moscow has repeatedly denied allegations of involvement in cyberattacks against European countries. No previous articleNo new articlesDaryna Antoniukis a reporter for Recorded Future News based in Ukraine. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. She previously was a tech reporter for Forbes Ukraine. Her work has also been published at Sifted, The Kyiv Independent and The Kyiv Post.

1s51bjz.text: The encrypted messaging platform Signal has announced it will by default stop users from taking screenshots of messages if they are using Google or Apple operating systems, a move fueled by concerns about how the tech giants deploy artificial intelligence agents. Last year, the widely used messaging app restricted Microsoft 11 users from screenshotting and keeping messages. Similar restrictions will now apply to Google’s Gemini Intelligence and Apple's Siri AI, Signal Foundation president Meredith Whittaker said in a Friday blog post. “These agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that’s making it increasingly hostile to privacy,” the blog post said. “This is an existential threat to Signal, and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission.” Whittaker said Signal plans to specifically restrict the agentic systems integrated into iOS 27 and versions of Android where Signal detects AI assistants trying to read text. The operating systems’ AI agents attempt to glean information from users by scanning what’s on their screens, Whittaker said, and in doing so hoover up the data in order to “answer your questions and do your bidding,” the blog post said. Whittaker warned the agents are making the captured data accessible to random local databases and remote servers at random. “All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation,” the blog post said. While screenshots won’t be permitted by default, the blog post said users who choose to can disable the block in settings. The “remedy is incomplete,” Whittaker warned, because blocking screenshots does not address “other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data, such as retrieving content already present on a user’s device via the filesystem.” The dearth of effective tools available to Signal and other app developers to use to stop AI agents from weakening privacy is a significant concern, the blog post said. Whittaker condemned Microsoft, Apple and Google for failing to provide app developers with a mechanism to block agents’ access to data without significantly compromising the “core user experience.” The same lack of cooperation from tech giants is also to blame for Signal’s inability to place the restrictions on macOS, the blog post said. Additionally, Signal has struggled with a profound lack of documentation about how the agents function. “Without better documentation and clear technical specifications, it will be increasingly difficult for Signal to provide robust privacy and security to the many millions of people who rely on us,” Whittaker said. “These three operating systems are the oceans in which Signal, and other applications, must swim; they dictate the conditions of life for the application ecosystem,” the blog post said of Apple, Google and Microsoft. “These agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that’s making it increasingly hostile to privacy.” Whittaker called on the companies to provide an easy way for users to opt-out of data access permissions tools, stop third-party agents from accessing data without users’ consent and bolster documentation lending transparency to how agents work. Apple did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Microsoft and Google declined to comment. Meta also has been under fire, following recent reports that its AI agent Muse broke into Signal conversations and digest them No previous articleNo new articlesSuzanne Smalley is a reporter covering digital privacy, surveillance technologies and cybersecurity policy for The Record. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

ls9zcs.text: Microsoft is warning customers that a security vulnerability in Azure API Management (APIM) Classic tiers was exploited to steal stored API credentials, with Norwegian authorities linking the flaw to cyberattacks against energy companies. Azure API Management is a cloud service that lets organizations publish, secure, monitor, and manage APIs that connect applications, services, and data. In an Azure Service Health security advisory (Tracking ID: MZK9-GH0) sent to customers and shared with BleepingComputer, Microsoft said it identified the vulnerability on November 18, 2026, and deployed a mitigation the following day. "Our investigation found that customers were exposed and an unauthorized party could have used the issue to access secrets stored in Azure API Management Classic instances before Microsoft identified the security issue," Microsoft said in the advisory. According to Microsoft, the vulnerability allowed unauthorized access to certain management functionality when APIM Classic instances were not configured according to recommended security best practices. This access could have allowed attackers to perform administrative operations, including accessing secrets stored in the service. Microsoft said the following information may have been exposed: Secrets stored in Named Values Client secrets associated with identity providers Client secrets associated with OpenID Connect providers Subscription keys Tokens used to call direct management APIs These credentials could potentially allow attackers to access additional applications, services, or backend systems, depending on their permissions. Microsoft said it closed the unauthorized access path on November 19 and rotated Microsoft-controlled keys and credentials where appropriate. However, the company warned that its remediation would not invalidate customer credentials that may have been compromised before the fix was deployed. "This remediation blocks the unauthorized management-plane access path that could allow an actor to perform administrative operations, including secrets management, against Azure API Management services," Microsoft warned. "However, it does not automatically invalidate credentials that may have been accessed before the fix was deployed." The vulnerability affects Azure API Management Classic tiers, while Microsoft said APIM v2 tiers are not impacted. Microsoft urged affected customers to immediately rotate potentially exposed credentials, investigate suspicious activity in systems accessible through those credentials, and review available logs for signs of unauthorized access. In a Reddit post, an administrator claimed their organization discovered the vulnerability after detecting unauthorized access to Azure Key Vault using a valid administrator token. "Our company has been fighting this for days, after discovering that someone logged into our keyvaults using a valid administrator token and not following the normal access pattern," the administrator claimed. The administrator alleged that attackers exploited a zero-day authentication bypass in a deprecated legacy API to gain access to a privileged system account on APIM instances. According to the administrator, the legacy API did not generate logs that customers could use to detect the unauthorized access. They also alleged that Microsoft initially attributed the suspicious activity to leaked customer credentials before deploying a global fix. BleepingComputer has not independently verified these allegations. The vulnerability has also been linked to attacks affecting Norwegian organizations, including energy companies Equinor and Skagerak Energi. In a security advisory, Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) said an unknown threat actor targeted access tokens, secrets, and named values stored in Azure API Management. The agency said Norway's energy sector first discovered the vulnerability and that organizations in other countries and industries were also affected. Equinor disclosed an ongoing cyberattack on November 17, a day before Microsoft says it identified the APIM vulnerability. The company later announced that it had stopped the attack and found no indication that data had been stolen or altered. Skagerak Energi also reported an attempted cyberattack but said it had no impact on its operations and no evidence that information was compromised. While Microsoft says it deployed a remediation on November 19 that required no customer action, NSM's advisory warns organizations to verify that their APIM instances have received the security update. The agency warns that instances running below specific runtime versions remain vulnerable and advises customers to contact their "service provider" if they have not received the update. It is unclear whether the runtime updates are separate from Microsoft's initial mitigation. Cloud security researcher Anders Kristiansen shared threat-hunting queries to help organizations investigate potential exploitation and identify credentials stored in their APIM instances. BleepingComputer contacted Microsoft with questions about the attacks but has not received a reply yet. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. 1vupeek.text: LaLiga, Spain's top men's professional football league, disclosed a data breach that exposed personal information belonging to users of its services and those of some affiliated clubs. According to the organization, the incident occurred between November 14 and 16, and the attacker extracted data from compromised systems. LaLiga organizes Spain’s top two men’s professional football divisions. The top league is one of the world’s most prominent football leagues, where clubs with a global audience, such as Real Madrid, FC Barcelona, and Atlético Madrid, play. On November 16, the organization’s security team identified the source of the unauthorized access and implemented measures to block the attack and stop the data extraction. “LALIGA was the target of a cyberattack on one of its technology platforms for fan services,” reads the announcement. “Between November 14 and 16, a cybercriminal gained unauthorized access to the platform and extracted personal data belonging to users registered for digital services offered by LALIGA and some clubs.” LaLiga underlined that the incident was confined to a specific platform and did not extend to other systems that support the running of the competitions. After implementing containment measures, LaLiga launched an investigation to determine the scope of the incident and introduced more thorough monitoring to detect future attempts to breach its systems. The football organizer also reported the incident to the Spanish Data Protection Agency (AEPD) and filed a complaint with the National Police’s Central Cybercrime Unit. Impacted clubs were also directly notified, and actions to inform impacted fans are being coordinated. At the time of writing, no ransomware group has claimed responsibility for the attack on LaLiga. BleepingComputer has contacted the organization to learn more about the attack and which clubs were impacted, but we have not received a response as of publication. 19m8w8h.text: The FBI is reportedly investigating a data breach involving the National Crime Information Center, a database used by U.S. law enforcement agencies that contains information on criminals, fugitives and missing people. The FBI did not respond to requests for comment but sources told CNN and later the Associated Press that the cyberattack took place on Thursday. The database, known as the NCIC, is used among local, state and federal agencies to share information on criminals and investigations. It offers law enforcement agencies data on outstanding warrants and contains sensitive information of value to criminals and others. President Donald Trump told Fox News this weekend that he had been briefed on the incident, adding: “I will say that it’s not good — I don’t like that.” He went on to say the breach may allow the public to have access to investigative files related to him. If confirmed, this would be the second cybersecurity incident affecting the FBI this year. In September, the ShinyHunters hacking group breached the FBI’s job site and allegedly stole troves of information on every FBI employee. Multiple people were arrested as part of the investigation into the ShinyHunters breach, including a cybersecurity expert from Canada. The U.S. government has suffered from several cybersecurity incidents this year in addition to the attacks on the FBI. Last month, hackers took down a platform used by all federal bankruptcy courts across the country and a ransomware attack in August targeted the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF). The ATF called the breach a “major incident” and said it involved a computer system containing information about targets of investigations. The departments of Defense and Transportation also experienced cybersecurity incidents this year, and the Department of Agriculture was forced to take offline multiple systems used to facilitate payments between the agency and farmers after a cyberattack last week.

eooxjz.text: Cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike will acquire cloud security company Zscaler for $43.9 billion in an all-stock deal announced on Monday morning. The deal will see two of the largest cybersecurity companies consolidate, merging Zscaler’s tools with CrowdStrike’s suite of cyberattack response services, endpoint security platforms, and threat intelligence offerings. Zscaler CEO Jay Chaudhry will continue to run Zscaler and will join CrowdStrike’s board of directors. CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz said the acquisition of Zscaler will allow them to build “cybersecurity’s operating system: a single control plane to deploy AI, control AI, and enable any agentic application to run safely.” “We see a path to become the largest AI safety and security company the world has ever seen,” he said. News of a potential acquisition emerged on Friday when Bloomberg reported that CrowdStrike was circling Zscaler, which had a market value of about $32 billion as of Friday. Zscaler shareholders will receive 1.135 shares of CrowdStrike common stock for each share of Zscaler common stock, or $260.41 per Zscaler share. Existing CrowdStrike shareholders are expected to own approximately 84.1% of Zscaler once the deal closes. CrowdStrike said the acquisition would allow it to sell its platforms to Zscaler’s 8,000 customers, including 50 percent of the Fortune 500. The company explained that while CrowdStrike’s tools focus on securing endpoints and data, Zscaler’s products are adept at “securing the connections between them.” “With Zscaler, CrowdStrike will enter network security, cybersecurity’s largest single addressable market segment,” a company spokesperson explained. Chaudhry warned that AI agents are “rapidly becoming the new weakest link” and said the deal with CrowdStrike will accelerate their ability to expand their zero trust tools to a larger customer base. “We see a significant opportunity to offer customers far superior protection in a rapidly evolving threat landscape and enable enterprises to safely adopt AI,” he said. Zscaler’s products will be sold through CrowdStrike’s system of resellers and distributors. Both companies released their quarterly earnings reports on Monday, with Zscaler reporting $949.3 million in revenue for the first quarter — a 20% increase compared to last year’s first quarter. The $43.9 billion figure tops last year’s largest deal, when Google purchased cloud security company Wiz for $32 billion. No previous articleNo new articlesJonathan Greigis a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

nc5a7u.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 23, 2026Cyber Espionage / Malware The China-aligned threat actor known as Webworm is suspected to be using a custom version of the open-source SoftEther VPN Bridge tool in an attempt to remove recognizable detection fingerprints, while disguising it as network-monitoring software to establish covert remote access to compromised networks. The modified variant "implements various tricks to hide itself from security tools," Rapid7 said in an analysis, attributing it to the adversarial collective with moderate confidence. First publicly detailed by Broadcom-owned Symantec in September 2022, Webworm is the name assigned to a China-aligned nation-state group that has targeted government entities, IT services, and electric power companies across Russia, Georgia, Mongolia, and several other Asian nations. One of the tools used by the threat actor is a legitimate software called SoftEther VPN, with the bridge acting as a pathway connecting the compromised network and the attacker-controlled infrastructure. The latest findings from Rapid7 revolve around a Windows executable ("netcapa.exe"), which is a modified build of SoftEther VPN Bridge ("vpnbridge_x64.exe") version 4.44, build 9807. The modified version, rebranded as NtMonitor VPN, masquerades itself as Network Monitor Software from a company called Network Systems Solutions Inc. The artifact was uploaded to VirusTotal around mid-January 2026. "The PDB path included in the executable reads C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\src\DebugFiles\pdb\x64_Release\vpnbridge.pdb," the cybersecurity company said. "As such, the tool doesn't hide its identity from reverse engineers, only external interactions." The renaming is also said to be inconsistent, with many registry key paths still referencing the program as "SoftEther Project," even though a number of other occurrences of "SoftEther VPN" have been replaced by "NtMonitor VPN." One of the most noticeable changes identified in the altered version is the use of innocuous-looking HTTP endpoints "/update/alive.cgi" and "/update/picture.cgi" to replace "/vpnsvc/vpn.cgi" and "/vpnsvc/connect.cgi," respectively, so that they look like ordinary web application activity. It also changes the protocol watermark used by SoftEther VPN as part of the handshake process when initiating communication to help the tool distinguish protocol traffic from ordinary HTTP requests. When the connecting client is found to speak the expected protocol, it proceeds with the handshake. If the check fails, the server returns a decoy HTTP response. The modified version swaps the GIF-based watermark used by the stock SoftEther VPN utility for a PNG-based watermark so as to bypass existing detection signatures based on the GIF watermark. Some of the other changes introduced to the program are listed below - Reducing a resource archive named hamcore.se2 used by SoftEther VPN to its bare minimum, as it's required to be present at runtime, and embedding it directly into the executable, causing the binary's size to increase by about 1.5 MB. Changing the name of the configuration file from "vpn_bridge.config" to "setting.conf" and making its contents encrypted with a custom algorithm. The encrypted configuration starts with the magic bytes "RCEN" in ASCII. What's interesting here is that the attackers have not been found to introduce any new functionality to the tool, indicating the primary focus was on stealth. "It seems like they methodically analyzed SoftEther's detection surface and implemented counter-measures to all of the easy ways a detection engineer may target it," Rapid7 said, calling the latest evolution a hybrid approach that brings together the attacker's use of custom malware and dual-use tools. "We are observing a sort of hybrid of the two — stock SoftEther software that is not trojanized, but rebuilt from source in a way that erases much of its detection fingerprint."

jpahyy.text: Editor's note: This article was updated with comment from Microsoft at 1:00 p.m. EST on Monday. Norwegian energy companies Equinor and Skagerak Energi are among the organizations affected by a Microsoft cloud security vulnerability that hackers have exploited to target sensitive credentials, Norway's cybersecurity authorities said. The vulnerability affected Azure API Management (APIM), a Microsoft service that allows organizations to manage and secure connections between applications and other systems. According to Norway's National Security Authority (NSM), an unidentified threat actor has been actively targeting access tokens and other sensitive information stored in the platform. Equinor, one of Europe's largest natural gas suppliers, and electricity producer Skagerak Energi both reported cyberattacks last week. The vulnerability was first discovered by Norway's energy sector, with Equinor playing a key role in identifying the issue and alerting authorities, the agency said on Friday. Equinor said it detected the attack last Tuesday but did not fully contain it until Friday. The incident disrupted some internal services, although the company's oil and gas production continued normally. "There is no indication that data has been stolen or altered," Equinor said in its latest statement, adding that the attack did not appear to have specifically targeted the company. Skagerak Energi, which produces and distributes electricity and is majority-owned by Norway's state-owned renewable energy company Statkraft, disclosed a separate cyberattack on Wednesday. The company said the incident had not affected its operations or electricity production and that it had found no indication that information had been compromised. In a non-public security advisory reportedly sent to customers and shared by a purported recipient on Reddit, Microsoft said it discovered on November 18 a security issue affecting the older “Classic” tiers of Azure API Management and closed the access path the following day. Microsoft warned that hackers may have accessed passwords and other sensitive information stored in vulnerable APIM systems before the company discovered the issue. The problem mainly affected customers who had not followed Microsoft's security recommendations or had stored sensitive information directly in APIM instead of using Azure Key Vault, a separate service designed to keep such data secure. Newer versions of APIM were not affected, the company said. Microsoft did not disclose how many customers may have been exposed or whether the same threat actor was responsible for the incidents involving the Norwegian energy companies. On Saturday, Microsoft published guidance explaining how affected customers could identify and replace potentially exposed credentials. The guidance did not explicitly acknowledge the vulnerability or link it to the Norwegian attacks. Microsoft told Recorded Future News it had identified and fixed a security flaw affecting several tiers of its Azure API Management service, including Developer, Basic, Standard and Premium. The company said it had notified potentially affected customers and provided guidance on how to protect their systems. A company spokesperson said they could not provide further details. Norwegian authorities said the vulnerability affected organizations across multiple sectors in Norway and abroad. "It remains unclear how extensively the vulnerability is being exploited or has been exploited in the past," said Martin Albert-Hoff, NSM's director of operational cybersecurity. He added that authorities had found no evidence that successful or attempted compromises had disrupted services at Norwegian organizations. NSM warned that more hackers could try to exploit the vulnerability now that it is publicly known and urged organizations using Azure API Management to take steps to protect their systems. "The national cyber risk level is high," Albert-Hoff said. "Incidents in recent weeks confirm that the risk of cyber operations remains elevated." No previous articleNo new articlesDaryna Antoniukis a reporter for Recorded Future News based in Ukraine. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. She previously was a tech reporter for Forbes Ukraine. Her work has also been published at Sifted, The Kyiv Independent and The Kyiv Post.

8l6o6g.text: A cyberattack disrupted operations at B2B top-up solutions provider GlobeTopper, causing an estimated $2.5 million in lost revenue, while the attacker redeemed digital gift cards worth $70,000. Parent company iQSTEL said that the intrusion was detected on October 22 and GlobeTopper responded by suspending its platform and starting an investigation. GlobeTopper is a business-to-business digital gift card distributor. Various retailers, fintech apps, and rewards platforms use its API. According to the platform’s website, it is used by more than 4,000 brands across 65 countries, including IKEA, Adidas, Spotify, Target, and Roblox. In a filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), iQSTEL said that GlobeTopper detected more unauthorized activity the day after it identified the attack. In response, the company "took the platform and all affected servers offline" in the early hours of October 23 to investigate and fix the problem. The company deployed a completely rebuilt platform on AWS on October 31, while commercial operations were restored in stages, starting November 1. GlobeTopper says the attacker obtained certain client API credentials and integration keys, which have been revoked and replaced, and it has observed no unauthorized use of them yet. “During its investigation, the Company determined that the unauthorized party obtained API credentials and integration keys of certain GlobeTopper business customers,” iQSTEL says. “All affected credentials and integration keys have been revoked and rotated, and affected business customers have been issued new credentials subject to additional access restrictions.” The company further stated that an investigation is ongoing to determine whether other customer, personal, payment, or provider data was accessed or acquired. Regarding the digital gift cards the attackers redeemed, the company says it cannot block, recover, or reclaim them, and will incur the losses. iQSTEL said the incident hurt GlobeTopper’s fourth-quarter transaction volume and operating results, but as of the filing, it has not determined it to be material. BleepingComputer has emailed iQSTEL with additional questions regarding the incident, but the company declined to share further information. At the time of writing, no ransomware groups have listed iQSTEL or GlobeTopper as victims on their extortion portals. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. henuhc.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 23, 2026Cybersecurity News / Hacking A stolen key. A trusted message. A routine update. None of these looks like the start of a major security problem. That's partly why they work. Attackers don't always need to break down a door. Sometimes they just use one that's already open. This week's stories show how quickly a small opening can turn into a much bigger mess. One breach helps attackers reach another target. Tools people rely on become ways to get inside. Even features built for safety can end up helping the wrong person. And some of the latest research shows just how little effort certain attacks need. The strange part is how normal it all looks until something goes wrong. A few attacks are clever. Others are almost embarrassingly simple. Both can do real damage. Here's what caught our attention this week. ⚡ Threat of the Week Threat Actor Exploits VMware vCenter Flaw as a 0-Day — The suspected China-nexus cyber espionage group known as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221) has been attributed to the zero-day exploitation of a critical security flaw in VMware vCenter Server in early September 2026. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS score: 9.8), is a case of authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service that could be exploited to gain unauthorized access to the system. In October, Google described a campaign by Armory Castle to exploit organizations through BeyondTrust's Remote Support tool, using a zero-day to breach the edge appliance and steal secrets useful for network reconnaissance and downstream compromises within organizations. The latest findings show that BeyondTrust was merely an entry point to a deeper and more complex campaign that involved the deployment of backdoors on Linux machines. 🔔 Top News Cursor Links Malicious Claude Extension Release to Fireworks AI Incident — Cursor has traced the origins of a security incident involving a malicious version of Anthropic's Claude Code extension in its marketplace to a breach at AI infrastructure provider Fireworks. "An attacker obtained an access key we had issued to Fireworks," Cursor said. "The key was exposed by Fireworks, and the attacker used it to copy data from a read-only storage bucket we used to share data with them." The Cursor incident is another indication of how the rapid adoption of AI-powered development tools and increasingly interconnected software ecosystems has worsened software supply chain risks. Cold Relic Exploits Cloud Breaches to Target Organizations — The Russian cyberespionage group known as Cold Relic is turning cloud breaches into a springboard for targeting a victim organization's wider network of trusted relationships. In the first intrusion observed late last year, the attackers gained control of a cloud administrator account and harvested internal communications, employee details, and other organizational records. Cold Relic later used that information to impersonate an employee of the first organization to conduct a social engineering attack on an individual at a second organization. The campaigns "demonstrate the convergence of human-centric social engineering and cloud identity abuse," Google said. "By obtaining access to strategic personnel rosters and operational documents, Russian intelligence services turn legitimate business communications into attack vectors against trusted partners." Malicious Web Pages Can Hijack Meta Muse — New research from the NebuSec research team has demonstrated that an attacker-controlled web page can be exploited to gain unauthorized access to user data associated with Meta Muse and compromise the underlying virtual machine (VM) in which it operates. "An attacker could retrieve conversation history and stored memories without triggering Muse's network approval prompts," NebuSec said. "The attack also allowed us to alter stored memories and conversation history, creating risks beyond unauthorized data access. By exploiting a vulnerability in the shared Linux kernel, we escaped the agent's runtime container and obtained root privileges in the underlying user VM." Meta has since addressed the issue. New FastUnlock Windows Narrator LockScreen Bypass Detailed — Security researcher Abdelhamid Naceri (aka Chaotic Eclipse) published FastUnlock, a new unpatched Windows 11 zero-day that abuses the Narrator screen reader to get past the lock screen and execute code as the lock screen account "WsiAccount." The attack requires physical access and at least one account linked to an online Microsoft account. GL.iNet GoodCloud Exploited to Serve Reverse Shells, Backdoors — Hackers have exploited a vulnerability in GL.iNet's GoodCloud cloud management platform to install malware, backdoors, and remote access tools on customers' routers and KVM devices."An unauthorized party exploited the vulnerability to access and install malicious software on some GL.iNet routers and KVM devices," GL.iNet said. "The attack path has been blocked. We fixed the cloud vulnerability and blocked the access used in this incident. Devices can no longer be newly infected through this attack path. The cloud-side fix alone does not remove malware from devices that were already infected." GL.iNet has not disclosed how the attackers exploited its cloud platform, how many customers were affected, or whether information was stolen as a result of these compromises. RemoteToHome said it examined 183 routers and found suspicious activity on 152, including 24 with root-level reverse shells, 47 with an older persistent backdoor, and 81 showing evidence that attacker-supplied commands had executed. It has also identified a potential command injection vulnerability in the GoodCloud client, although GL.iNet has not confirmed if this is the same vulnerability that was used in the attacks. ‎️‍🔥 Trending CVEs Bugs drop weekly, and the gap between a patch and an exploit is shrinking fast. These are the heavy hitters for the week: high-severity, widely used, or already being poked at in the wild. Check the list, patch what you have, and hit the ones marked urgent first — CVE-2026-14978, CVE-2026-45110, CVE-2026-49401, CVE-2026-59890 (Unicode Normalization Collision on macOS), CVE-2026-114938 aka Java4Shell (Java 17, 21, 25, and 27), CVE-2026-28400 (Docker Model Runner), CVE-2026-123633, CVE-2026-123007, CVE-2026-123634, CVE-2026-121810, CVE-2026-113425 aka NGINX2Root (NGINX and NGINX Plus), CVE-2026-120718 (F5 BIG-IP), CVE-2026-126822, CVE-2026-126336, CVE-2026-121812, CVE-2026-123637, CVE-2026-125272 (F5 BIG-IP APM), CVE-2026-120722, CVE-2026-121805, CVE-2026-120285, CVE-2026-120292, CVE-2026-116953 (F5 BIG-IP iRule), CVE-2026-125274 (F5 BIG-IP and BIG-IQ), CVE-2026-114819 (Oracle AI Database), CVE-2026-132825 aka Ruby2Shell (Ruby), CVE-2026-130963, CVE-2026-131031, CVE-2026-131060, CVE-2026-131008, CVE-2026-131054, CVE-2026-130975 (Google Chrome), CVE-2026-132165 (Drupal), CVE-2026-123890, CVE-2026-119618 (Broadcom VMware), CVE-2026-114202, CVE-2026-114204, CVE-2026-114205 (ASUS Control Center Express Agent), CVE-2026-126574 (ASUS Control Center), CVE-2026-112115 (ASUS Armoury Crate), CVE-2026-99312, CVE-2026-99362 (Linux kernel), CVE-2026-132798 (Temenos Application Framework Java), CVE-2026-134624 (N-able Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud), CVE-2026-131914 (Idunno.AntiCsrf), CVE-2026-125396 aka Upload2Shell (Ghostscript), CVE-2026-129975 (GPGME), GHSA-qc22-rmgc-vg94 (MONAI Label), CVE-2026-23871 (WhatsApp for Android and WhatsApp Business for Android), and CVE-2026-134814 (binary-parser). 🎥 Cybersecurity Webinars 6,000 Social Engineering Attacks Reveal Why MFA Still Fails to Stop Account Takeovers → AI-powered phishing and voice scams are evolving, while attackers exploit weaker authentication and recovery paths to bypass MFA. Join this webinar to uncover real attack techniques and learn how to prevent account takeovers. 8 Million Security Events Reveal Why Attackers Can Hide Behind Tools You Already Trust → Attackers abuse legitimate IT tools to evade detection, but only about 12 in a million uses are malicious. Join this webinar to learn how to distinguish real threats from normal activity without drowning in alerts. Your GitHub Actions Are SHA-Pinned. But Are They Actually Secure? → SHA pinning locks code to a commit, but doesn't verify its author or origin. Attackers can exploit this trust gap to sneak malicious code past security checks. Join this webinar to learn how impostor commits threaten CI/CD pipelines and how to defend against them. 📰 Around the Cyber World Google Cloud-owned VirusTotal has introduced new cipher-agnostic file-encryption verification across Windows and macOS sandboxes to check whether a suspicious file actually encrypts user documents upon execution. This has led to the detection of a .k404 extortion campaign that managed to go undetected by 75 static antivirus engines, while its companion binary ("K404T_Fidye.exe") only had 10 / 75 detections. The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) has warned that threat actors can abuse an authenticated WhatsApp Web session to gain unauthorized access to a user's account, allowing them to read messages, send messages while impersonating the user, and misuse the identity of the account holder for fraud, phishing, social engineering, or other malicious activities. Users are advised to log out of sessions when not required and avoid signing in using public computers. A large-scale malvertising operation dubbed MoldyRoost that's leveraging advertising infrastructure to deliver iPhone exploit chain kits like Coruna, DarkSword, SilkPath (iOS 17.2.2 to 18.3), and GhostWave (iOS 18.7.3 to 26) with an aim to exfiltrate crypto wallet seed phrases, iCloud Keychain data, messages, and photos. "Just loading the landing page of a MoldyRoost ad on a vulnerable iPhone is enough to get infected," Confidant said. "The exploit runs while the landing page loads, with no decoy download or ClickFix-style command to paste. What MoldyRoost adds is expertise in distributing the exploit kits through malvertising." Only an iOS device running Safari is offered an exploit chain. Other devices are served a working decoy website, an empty frame, or a harmless landing page. More than 480 domains have been linked to the operation between May 12 and November 17, 2026. The activity has targeted over 47 countries, mainly Hong Kong, Japan, Singapore, the U.S., South Korea, the U.K., and India. The average time from an infostealer infection to the threat actor logging in via the same credentials is only eight minutes in some cases, according to a report from Elastic Security Labs. Unknown threat actors have siphoned an estimated $133 million from Crédit Mutuel Arkéa by using the bank’s own account to wire the funds to other banks, from where it was potentially converted into cryptocurrency. "The attackers used Crédit Mutuel Arkéa's own account to make transactions to other banking institutions, which then potentially allowed them to convert this money into cryptocurrency via specialized platforms," the bank said, adding the attackers did not go through the accounts of customers at its federations or subsidiaries. Uber has confirmed that nearly 150,000 people had their personal information compromised after hackers broke into one of its AI suppliers. A filing with Oregon's Attorney General puts the number of victims at 149,346. The access data includes images of drivers' licenses and information extracted from them, including names, home addresses, dates of birth, and license numbers. Arion Kurtaj, a 21-year-old member of the LAPSUS$ group, pleaded guilty in a U.K. court to hacking Rockstar Games, Uber, BT, and Revolut, after being released from a secure hospital after he was deemed fit to stand trial. He was originally sentenced to an indefinite stay at a hospital due to the severity of his autism. Browser extensions associated with Lacuna Web PKI, Softplan Web Signer, Certisign WebSigner, Certisign CertiPlugin, and BRy Assinatura Digital have been found to be rife with critical vulnerabilities rated 9.6 on the CVSS scoring system. These digital signing extensions are used by millions of government agencies and legal, medical, and tax professionals. "All five make the same mistake, they let the website choose which DLL the vendor's native host loads," Bay Area Labs said. "Loading a DLL runs its code and the software built to verify signatures never checked the signature on the code it loaded and on Web PKI and CertiSign WebSigner, a malicious page or iframe, such as an ad, was enough, with no click. On Softplan Web Signer, opening a link was enough. On CertiPlugin and BRy, visiting the page was enough, and the page downloaded the payload automatically." The bug class has been codenamed Sign2Shell. The flaws could have allowed fraudsters to sign legal documents in victims' names and potentially breach major organizations. The issues have since been fixed. Anthropic has become the latest company to cut its coordinated vulnerability disclosure window from 90 to 30 days for high- and critical-severity issues, and to 45 days for all other issues, as AI collapses bug discovery timelines. The new deadlines cover reports sent on or after January 1, 2027. Recovery from a ransomware attack takes a median time of 20 days, and nearly a third of victims require more than six weeks. "Only 32% were recovered within two weeks and 28% took longer than six weeks," Rubrik said. "The full case, measured until the customer was content to close it, had a median of 26 days and 45% of cases stayed open for more than 30 days." Fortra said it's tracking targeted, large-scale "mail bombing" attacks, followed immediately by IT support impersonation on Microsoft Teams. "In the attacks, individual users are being flooded with email, then contacted by the threat actor through Teams as the volume peaks," Fortra said. "In the calls, the threat actors are claiming to be representatives from Internal IT, providing the user both verbal and email instructions they claim will stop the flood, but in reality attempting to compromise the user account, system, or both." Tyler Robert Buchanan, 24, of Dundee, Scotland, has been sentenced to six years in prison in the U.S. for his role in conspiring to hack into at least a dozen companies' computer systems via smishing attacks and steal over $11.6 million in virtual currency from individual victims throughout the U.S. A member of the Scattered Spider group, Buchanan pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and one count of aggravated identity theft in April 2026. He was arrested in Spain in June 2024 and extradited to the U.S. in April 2025. Igor Andreevich D'iu, a 25-year-old Russian national, has been indicted in the U.S. for allegedly acting as a spy of a foreign government to "conduct surveillance and gather information about employees of a Silicon Valley technology and defense company." Although the name of the company was not disclosed, it's understood to be Palantir Technologies. D'iu was arrested on October 30, 2026. "The allegations in this case describe a state-sponsored operation to target and harass employees of an American technology and defense company because of that company's assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia," said United States Attorney Craig H. Missakian. He is said to have entered the U.S. illegally through Mexico in June 2026 and was instructed by co-conspirators on Telegram to "identify company employees, and photograph their laptop screens while they worked," as well as "include surveillance of company employees and their residences." At least $247 million of the stolen funds from the record-breaking Binance hack has now gone into coinjoins coordinated by Kruw to obscure the financial trail, Elliptic has revealed. "Almost all of these coinjoins were coordinated by Kruw, the most widely used coordinator for Wasabi Wallet users," the company said. "A coordinator organizes each coinjoin round, bringing together the users taking part, but never takes custody of their funds." Last week, blockchain investigator ZachXBT accused Kruw of knowingly helping the Lazarus Group launder stolen cryptocurrency assets, calling the threat actor their "largest" user. Arkham Intelligence has also identified 2,173.76 BTC, roughly $154.45 million, flowing into CoinJoin from wallets connected to the $387 million Bitget hack of September 2025, also linked to North Korea. Kruw.io was also the subject of an advisory issued by the U.S. Secret Service in May 2025. "Numerous illicit actors use Kruw.io to launder funds including the Lazarus Group, a North Korean hacking collective also known as АPТ38 and TraderTraitor which is subject to U.S. and international sanctions," the advisory said. "The Lazarus Group has previously used Kruw.io to mix approximately $14.3 million in cryptocurrency stolen by the North Korean regime. The Lazarus Group is currently laundering some proceeds of the $1.5 billion Bybit hack through the Kruw.io service." Conclusion The tricky part isn't always finding the problem. It's knowing how far it has already spread. A stolen login can lead to another company. A fixed bug can leave infected devices behind. And a tool that worked fine yesterday might be the reason someone gets in tomorrow. There isn't always a clean ending once the damage is done. That's it for this week's recap. Some of these stories need a closer look. Others are useful reminders to check the things we tend to trust without thinking. Either way, there's plenty here worth keeping an eye on. See you next week, hopefully with fewer surprises.

11hm4t6.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 23, 2026Vulnerability / Open Source A critical security flaw has been disclosed in the popular binary-parser library that could allow an attacker who controls parser definitions to execute arbitrary code. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-134814 (CVSS score: 9.2 / 8.1), is a case of code injection impacting binary-parser versions prior to 2.3.1. "Binary-parser before 2.3.1 contains a code injection vulnerability that allows attackers controlling parser definitions to inject JavaScript through string-typed options passed unvalidated by Context.generateOption()," according to a description of the flaw in the NIST National Vulnerability Database (NVD). "Attackers can supply crafted length, lengthInBytes, key, tag, offset, or namely() alias values to execute arbitrary JavaScript in the Node.js process when the parser is compiled." According to an advisory released by the project maintainer on November 11, 2026, the problem arose from the fact that some user-controlled string options were inserted directly into the generated JavaScript code without adequate validation. The parser options include - length lengthInBytes key tag offset, and the alias passed to namely() "Parsing untrusted binary data with a trusted parser definition is not affected," Keichi Takahashi, who maintains the library, said. "These options are now validated as identifier paths (e.g. foo, $parent.len). Expressions such as 'len - 1' are rejected; use a function instead." CVE-2026-134814 can also be viewed as an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-1245 (CVSS score: 6.5), another code injection vulnerability that was fixed back in January 2026 and resulted from insufficient validation of field names and encoding parameters. "[The flaw] allows attackers controlling parser definitions to inject and execute arbitrary JavaScript within the host Node.js process upon parser compilation," Upwind Security said in an X post. Users are advised to update to the latest version of the library for optimal protection.

1aprlgy.text: Frontier AI labs are very clear about their responsibilities: making the model more robust, better guarded, and harder to hijack. They are also clear about what they can’t do, which is understand the business context of an action. An agent deleting files from Google Drive could be malicious or perfectly normal. They can't tell. That raises questions about the shared responsibility model for Agentic AI. In cloud security, there is a clear separation of responsibilities between cloud vendors and their customers. If you copy data from AWS into SFDC, each vendor is responsible for the data's infrastructure security while they have it, but the customer is responsible for the action. The AWS Shared Responsibility Model is a classic example. The separation isn’t nearly as clean for AI agents. Agents act as intermediaries between you and the request, and that intermediary isn't deterministic by nature. It sends authenticated, authorized requests that can be compromised or rogue. The first scenario is somewhat clear and goes back to what the AI labs try to prevent: a rogue agent has either misunderstood something or acted in a way it shouldn’t. A human mistake, only not human and not necessarily a mistake. Five organizations have published guidance on responsibility for AI agents: shared responsibility models from Microsoft, CSA and CoSAI, AWS's security guidance for AgentCore, and Anthropic's “Trustworthy agents in practice.” Only two assign ownership of an agent’s identity, and they split it differently. No one agrees on who is responsible for the agent's behavior. A look at the existing approaches The available guidance approaches responsibility from different angles. Some publications assign specific tasks to providers and customers; others describe security layers or broader stakeholder roles. Together, they show why organizations need to determine who owns each agent, what permissions it has, and how it operates across the systems it uses. Company Description Focus Microsoft Publishes an AI agent shared responsibility model with a matrix for IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS deployments. The customer remains accountable for agent actions across all three models. Agent identity and delegated token management, along with per-action authorization checks, are customer responsibilities in IaaS and shared responsibilities in PaaS and SaaS. AWS No agent-specific model, but AgentCore's security guidance applies AWS's general shared responsibility model. Closest match: the Agentic AI Security Scoping Matrix and its NIST comment. Builders bear final responsibility for the behavior and permissions of the systems they assemble. AWS recommends enforcing security through infrastructure-level controls outside the agent and discusses agent identity, credentials, and delegation. Anthropic “Trustworthy agents in practice” describes four layers of an agent system: model, harness, tools, and environment. It does not provide a formal responsibility matrix. Calls for defenses across all four layers and asks customers to consider which tools, permissions, and environments they give agents. In a separate NIST response, Anthropic identifies authentication and permissions across agent boundaries as an unresolved challenge. CSA Agent Shared Security and Safety Responsibility Model (Agent 3SRM) maps the CSA AI Controls Matrix to a ten-layer agent architecture. Its public summary introduces an Agent Owner with ultimate, non-delegable accountability for agent actions and addresses accountability for sub-agent delegation. The summary does not detail its identity and authorization assignments. CoSAI The AI Shared Responsibility Framework V1.0 uses five layers, responsibility matrices, and autonomy levels L0 to L5. Its general principle calls for one accountable party per component, and its identity and access management matrix assigns accountability to the end user or organization. Its autonomy guidance also describes shared accountability between the agentic provider and application developer at L4 to L5, creating an apparent tension with that principle. Let's say it goes wrong Consider a coding agent that reads a support ticket through an MCP server. That ticket contains malicious instructions that cause the agent to push a change to GitHub using the developer's token. It isn't a contrived case. In the organizations Token monitors, 60% of Claude Code and Desktop agents called two or more outside vendors, and 47% called three or more, in the span of one month. Now to the million-dollar question: who's responsible for catching the malicious push and stopping it? Could it be the harness? The software that runs the agent has the most visibility: it knows where the instructions were (albeit not why they were there) and the command about to run. Claude Code, for example, checks both. A server-side probe "scans incoming tool results and flags suspicious content before Claude reads it." In auto mode, now the starting mode for interactive sessions, a separate classifier blocks actions that appear "driven by hostile content Claude read." OpenAI, Cursor, and GitHub each have their own versions of approval prompts, automated reviewers, network limits, and sandboxes. This capability doesn't come with responsibility, though. Harnesses put that squarely on the user's shoulders, both within the interface and in their terms. Will the MCP catch it? The poisoned ticket came in over MCP, a protocol built for model clients. You might expect it to carry some of the load, because it's a door purpose-made for agents. At least conceptually, it could denote expanded responsibility for the people who built this door. The MCP spec hands the load back to the client. Clients SHOULD validate tool results before passing them to the model, and "there SHOULD always be a human in the loop with the ability to deny tool invocations," it says. The server's duties involve tokens, inputs, access controls, and rate limits. And so, a typical MCP server will check who sent a request, not whether it should have been sent. It all goes back to the MCP spec, which neither uses the term "prompt injection" nor provides the server with any verified information about its caller; client information is "self-reported." It says outright that "MCP itself cannot enforce these security principles at the protocol level." Atlassian, for its part, calls the use of MCP clients with its products "a customer-elected action." Could GitHub be the solution? The push reaches GitHub with a valid token. Unless an admin has set up a branch protection rule for main, nothing stops it, and by default, those rules "don't apply to people with admin permissions to the repository." GitHub's audit log includes an agent marker, actor_is_agent, for agents that run on GitHub. Nothing in the docs says it marks a local agent's push, though. And the terms are the same as everyone's: "You are responsible for all content posted and activity that occurs under your Account." Do agent identities close the gap? In an ideal scenario, every agent has its own identity, which should carry narrower, shorter-lived access. Microsoft, for example, gives agents identities of their own: a Microsoft Entra agent identity is a service principal in your Entra tenant. Microsoft's framework also marks per-action authorization as shared. But when an agent acts on behalf of a user, Microsoft's documentation says "risky activity is attributed to the user." A Conditional Access policy aimed at an agent identity "doesn't cover agent requests made on behalf of the user." And that's the story in a nutshell, within one vendor. Even if the framework points to shared responsibility, the product attributes the risk to the user when it's actually time to act. You share the responsibility That leaves you. And it's probably going to remain the norm. While platforms could, in theory, do more, agents are considered extensions of our will, even though they often have a “will” of their own. It's a novel scenario, and the only choice is to look at the risk honestly and decide how much of it we're willing to accept. And even that is easier said than done because you can't see the agent as a single thing. The harness has its telemetry, Atlassian has its MCP log, and GitHub has the developer's push. Coding agents like this one run under the developer's credentials by default, so their actions appear to be the developer's. No vendor in this chain sees the whole agent: The harness sees the instruction The MCP server sees a token GitHub sees a developer pushing code Only the identity the agent uses crosses all three. That makes it the one place where a single owner can set scope, expiry, and revocation. Branch protection and allowlists help, but identity ties them together. What to do about it Ideally, you treat the agent as one identity, whatever number of vendors it touches: Inventory per agent, across vendors. For each agent, list credentials. Give agents identities of their own, scoped to the task and short-lived. Decide where your log trail for agentic decision-making and action lives. Turn on branch protection, read-only modes, tool allowlists, and everything else that can help. Build a revocation path and practice killing an agent's access across all vendors. Ask your vendors what they can show you about an agent that also acts elsewhere. An organization cannot delegate accountability for an agent’s actions to a model provider or infer intent from an authenticated request. It can assign an owner, limit the agent’s access, connect its activity across systems, and test how to stop it. Those decisions make agent adoption governable without assuming any single vendor can see the whole workflow. If the responsibility is yours, it pays to be responsible. When you’re ready to secure your AI Agents for growth, book a demo with the Token Security team. Sponsored and written by Token Security.

1ssinmv.text: Threat actors are exploiting a now-patched security flaw in ConnectWise ScreenConnect to target managed service provider (MSP) servers. The activity revolves around CVE-2026-84869 (CVSS score: 9.9), a critical ScreenConnect client flaw that allows a guest to transfer and execute a malicious payload on a connecting technician's host. "On November 12, 2026, we observed one managed service provider's (MSP) technician's workstation exploited to run a guest-pushed batch file, which then reported to a Telegram bot, downloaded an installer from masterdarky[.]com, and started a rogue ScreenConnect client pointing at the attacker's own relay, all in about 9 seconds," Huntress security researcher John Hammond said. The batch script, "update_224ac089.bat," is designed to decode a Base64 Telegram bot token and chat ID, and register the new infection. Subsequently, it downloads an MSI installer that masquerades as a Windows update ("WindowsUpdate.msi") to launch a ScreenConnect client, enabling the attacker to gain remote access to the technician's machine. The activity, observed between October 20 and November 16, 2026, is said to have sprayed servers blindly, with Huntress observing at least 688,000 guest "run file" requests for files named update.bat or update_<8 hex>.bat hitting 42 ScreenConnect servers from 29 IP addresses. The guests have been found to make repeated requests that have blank session names or default-looking Windows hostnames. In another instance, a guest machine at 91.224.92[.]167 pushed a seemingly harmless text file ("marker.txt") two seconds after a technician joined a session, effectively acting as a canary to alert the operator that the exploit works against the target before sending the actual payload. What's more, a targeted attack aimed at an MSP server in October 2026 had the attacker joining as a guest across three real sessions the technician had created and asked the client to run a file designed to drop a batch script ("Sync.bat") into the technician's computer's Windows Startup folder. It's worth noting that this activity is distinct from a recently disclosed attack wave in which unknown threat actors gained unauthorized access to partner ScreenConnect environments by leveraging an authentication flaw in a third-party extension to deploy a malware toolkit called SCKit, which then exploits the flaw to propagate the malware to a technician's workstation. The attacks also coincide with another cluster in which thousands of unauthorized ScreenConnect guest sessions have originated from machines with cryptocurrency exchange-themed names like BITMEX-BOT, KUCOIN-SRV, and LAPTOP-BINANCE to trick technicians into connecting to them. No following malicious activity such as file transfers or command execution has been observed. Specifically, the threat actors have been found to obtain access to publicly downloadable ScreenConnect Access installers to extract the relay address needed to register a guest client with the corresponding ScreenConnect server, and then create fake guest sessions and make those sessions appear online. "Someone is registering unauthorized guest computers on MSPs' servers, where they sit in these session lists. They come from a scripted emulator that impersonates a Windows ScreenConnect client, and nearly all of them had connected from a single IONOS-hosted IP, 74.208.158[.]106," Huntress said. "As of November 13, we've seen related activity across at least 118 self-hosted ScreenConnect servers belonging to 109 Huntress-protected organizations. In total, we found 2,408 unauthorized sessions enrolled since November 3, 2026." Organizations are advised to ensure that technicians' ScreenConnect host clients are updated to 26.6.5 or later, hunt for signs of exposure, isolate affected workstations, and rotate all credentials reachable from that workstation. If immediate patching is not feasible, it's recommended to remove the TransferFiles permission from roles and session groups. "An MSP technician's workstation typically holds RMM consoles, saved credentials, and access to every customer, making it an exceptionally attractive target," Huntress said. "When a technician joins a remote session, their ScreenConnect host client and the guest machine can exchange files. Normally, the technician decides what moves and what runs." "A malicious guest exploiting CVE-2026-84869 can push a file to the technician's machine and get the technician's own client to run it. From the technician's view, no prompt appears. They only have to join the session, whether from an attacker-controlled machine or a real customer's support session that the attacker has slipped into as an extra guest."

tdfwc1.text: Microsoft is working to fix a long-standing Windows issue that has been causing significant audio quality drops for Bluetooth headphone users. This is triggered when Windows automatically switches from the headphone (A2DP stereo) profile to the headset (hands-free, phone-call-like) profile when an app or game activates and uses the headset's microphone, because bandwidth is limited in two-way mode. After installing the preview builds released for the Beta and Experimental channels on Friday, Windows 11 Insiders with newer Bluetooth headsets can keep playing high-quality audio even after the OS switches between profiles. "Bluetooth LE Audio devices can now play at full-range stereo fidelity while also using the device's microphone, ensuring you continue to hear great audio quality when in game chat, in a voice call, using voice typing, or using voice chat in Copilot Chat," said Windows Insider communications lead Stephen Lines. "When using an LE Audio device with a PC that supports Super Wideband Stereo, choose the new 2 channels, 16 bit, 48000Hz option from Settings > System > Sound > Output > {Bluetooth device} > Output settings > Format when microphone is active." This new feature is available for all Bluetooth LE Audio devices that support 48kHz playback, such as headphones, earbuds, and speakers. Bluetooth LE Audio format settings (Microsoft) ​Earlier this month, Microsoft also fixed USB audio issues that have plagued Windows users who installed security updates released since September. As it explained when it acknowledged this known issue days after the September 2026 Patch Tuesday, USB Audio Class 1.0 devices failed to start or produce audio on some systems after installing recent updates. Two years ago, Microsoft also blocked Windows 24H2 upgrades on systems with incompatible Intel Smart Sound Technology (SST) audio drivers due to blue screen of death (BSOD) issues and confirmed an issue that was causing game audio to go full volume when using USB DAC sound systems. In January 2025, Microsoft addressed a bug causing audio playback problems and Code 10 errors on Windows 11 24H2 systems with USB audio device drivers after installing the KB5050094 preview update. More recently, on Tuesday, Microsoft announced that it's testing a new feature that lets IT admins remotely lock stolen or lost enterprise Windows devices without wiping them. eax96a.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 23, 2026Vulnerability / Cloud Security N-able yesterday disclosed a critical flaw it found while investigating the breach of its Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud, an email filtering service it runs for managed service providers. The bug, tracked as CVE-2026-134624, is a server-side request forgery (SSRF) flaw. It allowed a user with high-level API access to open connections to internal systems of the user's choosing on the platform's servers. The company fixed the flaw and restored access to the dashboard and APIs late on Saturday, closing an outage that began last Monday. Email delivery and spam filtering kept working throughout, according to the company. It has not said whether the flaw was the attackers' way in. The bug sat in a connection check that Mail Assure runs for LDAP synchronization when a relay is configured. Before the fixed build, nothing restricted that check's destination, so the server could be pointed at any internal host and port to see which ones answered. "An authenticated API user can cause the server to connect to arbitrary internal hosts and ports, determine which are reachable, and send crafted data to internal services.," the vendor's security advisory says. The advisory gives the flaw a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.3, and lists builds earlier than 20261121.1943 as affected, with that same build as the fix. It does not claim code execution. N-able informed customers of a service disruption last Monday and initially traced it to platform configuration and service dependencies, according to its incident timeline. Last Wednesday, the company said the outage was, in fact, a security incident: an unauthorized party had accessed one of the Hosted Cloud servers. The dashboard and APIs were kept offline as a precaution while it investigated. It responded by taking the affected server offline, rotating internal platform credentials, revoking customers' existing API tokens, invalidating OAuth tokens, and resetting local users' passwords. The company says it has found no evidence that customer data was compromised, including tenants' mailboxes, and no sign of exploitation beyond that one server since the fix was implemented. The investigation is still open, and the breach is unrelated to the N-central incident, according to the company. In that earlier incident, it took its hosted remote-monitoring platform offline on November 9 after a researcher published 33 unpatched flaws. For hosted customers, the work now is reconnecting. Scripts and integrations that used the revoked API tokens or OAuth tokens will need new credentials. The exact steps differ by setup: each partner has been emailed guidance specific to its environment, and anyone who has not received it is asked to contact support. The hosted platform itself is already patched, according to yesterday's incident update, so there is nothing for Hosted Cloud users to install. SpamExperts Local Cloud runs on customer hardware, with software updates applied on a weekly schedule, according to the product's update documentation. The incident statements describe the Hosted Cloud only, so Local Cloud operators should confirm their servers are on build 20261121.1943. What the account so far does not say is how the attackers first got in, or whether any of the credentials they may have reached were actually taken. An outside digital forensics and incident response team has been brought in, and the company says a formal root cause analysis is due within two weeks of yesterday's update. Separate restoration times for quarantine, logging, and mailbox synchronization, which were being brought back in phases, have not been given.

1a75awl.text: A Peruvian call center operator was sentenced to eight years in prison for helping steal millions of dollars from over 30,000 Spanish-speaking US residents in a years-long government-impersonation fraud scheme. 45-year-old Carla Magaly Alcedo Mendoza of Lima, Peru, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit mail and wire fraud after being charged in an 18-count indictment following her March 2023 arrest and April 2025 extradition to the United States. According to court documents, Alcedo managed and operated Peruvian call centers linked to multiple large-scale fraud and extortion schemes between January 2013 and December 2018. The scammers first contacted Spanish-speaking Americans, claiming they qualified for free services or products. However, they later impersonated US government officials and lawyers and told the victims they were contractually obligated to pay large sums of money to receive them. Together with her accomplices, she defrauded and extorted thousands of Americans by falsely threatening them with court action, arrest, and immigration consequences in unsolicited phone calls targeting Spanish-speaking Americans. "The scheme spanned several years and thousands of victims made payments to Alcedo. Collectively, the scheme was responsible for defrauding more than 30,000 Spanish-speaking residents of the United States out of $15 million," the Department of Justice said. "These criminals preyed on hardworking Americans, using fear and intimidation to steal millions of dollars. They deliberately targeted Spanish-speaking communities, impersonating government officials and threatening innocent people with arrest and legal consequences," added Acting US Attorney Yara Lorenzo Klukas. Alcedo was the tenth defendant extradited from Peru and sentenced in this scheme, with ten other Peruvian call center owner-operators and four distribution center owner-operators involved in the scheme convicted so far. This follows a June 2026 warning from the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) that Americans have lost $3.5 billion to impersonation scams in 2025, with reported losses nearly tripling since 2020 and approximately $920 million stolen by government impersonators. In April, the FBI also warned in its 2025 Internet Crime Report that US victims lost nearly $21 billion to cyber-enabled crimes throughout last year.
